Cpt_2034.t: Homily on the weakness of the flesh
Cpt_2034.c: Papyrus fragment preserving a homily on the weakness of the flesh, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2036.c: Eleven papyrus fragments, some with Coptic text on both sides, some with text on one side only, and some blank, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments were written by at least four different scribes. Many appear to be Christian; one fragment mentions Abraham and God and another mentions a priest.

Cpt_2037.c: Eleven papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. At least three different scribes, and one fragment is written in a business hand.

Cpt_2038.c: Six papyrus fragments from two unrelated folios, with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment contains the words 'kingdom' and 'he blessed'.

Cpt_2040.c: Two unrelated papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. One fragment mentions angel names and the other mentions the cross of Christ.

Cpt_2041.c: Two papyrus fragments from a literary codex with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt (possibly Thebes). The larger fragment is paginated: Λ (30).

Cpt_2042.c: Sixteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments are probably all from the same papyrus manuscript or document.

Cpt_2043.c: Fifteen papyrus fragments with Coptic or Greek texts on one side only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2044.t: Papyrus fragments from Athanasius' letter to Dracontius
Cpt_2044.c: Nine papyrus fragments from a roll, with Coptic texts on the front only. The fragments preserve a portion of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius (see Cpt 2047), from a scroll in the Montserrat collection (P . Monts Roca inv. 14), written in Coptic in the 4th century in Egypt.

Cpt_2045.c: Nineteen papyrus fragments from a codex written in two columns, with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments include portions of the Passion homily (Peri Pasha) of Melito of Sardis, from what is known as the 'Crosby-Schoyen codex' (MS 193) (see Cpt 2046).

Cpt_2046.c: Twenty-four papyrus fragments preserving unidentified literary texts (most blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2047.c: Forty-seven papyrus fragments preserving some portions of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius dated to the 4th century AD (see Cpt 2044) and other unidentified literary texts (many blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2048.c: Fragment of a papyrus folio from a codex, with Fayyumic Coptic text on front and back in two columns, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The text contains authoritative pronouncements about Sunday.

Cpt_2049.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a letter
Cpt_2049.c: Eight papyrus fragments written in Coptic cursive scribe on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt, possibly preserving portions of a private letter.

Cpt_2050.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a homily
Cpt_2050.c: Twenty-five papyrus fragments from a roll with Coptic text on the recto only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. As Easter is mentioned the fragments may preserve part of a homily, perhaps Melito's Paschal Homily.

Cpt_2051.c: Two papyrus fragments with Greek and Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment is written in Coptic and includes a gloss with 'faith, hope, charity' written in the upper margin and 'Moses, Solomon, David' in the left margin. The lower fragment is written in Greek, with different orientations on either side, 'Christ' is written on one and 'the kingdom of ... on earth' is written on the other side.

Cpt_2052.c: Papyrus fragments preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2053.c: Four papyrus fragments from two different folios preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2054.c: Four papyrus fragments with Coptic and Greek texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Three fragments are written in Coptic including one with text from Mark 1.21, and one which is paginated; one fragment is written in Greek and mentions bread.

Cpt_2055.t: Parchment fragments from a homily citing Revelation 4
Cpt_2055.c: Fifteen parchment fragments with Coptic text on back and front, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve part of a homily citing Revelation 4; from a codex written in two columns. Evidence of damage from a fire.

Cpt_2056.c: Papyrus fragment from an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2059.c: Twenty-three papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 8: 6.9-10, 14-15 and pagination; frag 6: 11.1-2, 6-7; frag 9: 11.49-52, 53-12.3 and 2 Corinthians (frag 2: 4.12-17, 18-5.4; frag 12: 6.17-7.4, 5-8), and pagination; and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2060.c: Twenty-one papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 21: 2:38, 43-44 and pagination; frag 10: 3.7-13, 14-4:2 and pagination) and pagination (frags 11 and 22), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2061.c: Thirty-one papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frags 17/13: 1.59-60, 61-62, 67-68, 68-69; frag 5: 2.38-39, 43-44; frags 1/7: 3.1-2, 5-8; frag 6: 5.10, 14; frag 8: 12.42, 47-48) and 2 Corinthians (frag 3: 2.15-16, 3.3-4; frag 2: 12.6-7, 10-12), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2062.c: Nine papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 7: 5.25-27, 30-32; frag 5: 9.18-19, 22; frags 2/4: 11.48-52, 53-12.3) and 2 Corinthians (frag 6: 5.10-11, 15-16; frag 1: 8.10-14, 14-20 and pagination); and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2063.t: Papyrus fragments including Luke 1.63, 1.70; 4.8, 13-15; 4.28-29, 34 and 2 Corinthians title, 1.1, 1.6; 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 11.22, 26
Cpt_2063.c: Fourteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve pagination and titling including portions of Luke (frag 9: 1.63, 1.70; frag 10: 4.8, 13-15; frag 13: 4.28-29, 34), pagination (frags 11 and 7) and 2 Corinthians (frag 12: title, 1.1, 1.6; frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frag 2: 11.22, 26), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2064.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 2.18-21, 23-25 and 2 Corinthians 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8
Cpt_2064.c: Four papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 2.18-21, 23-25) and 2 Corinthians (frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frags 1 and 3: 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2065.c: Papyrus fragments preserving the Martyrdom of St Cephalon, an unknown Coptic martyr, executed under the prefect of Egypt, Clodius Culcianus. Text written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 6th or 7th century AD. Text on both sides (presumably continuous) suggests the fragment originally formed part of a codex. The text features the prefect presiding over the martyr's trial, Cephalon the martyr, and a third figure whose name is broken, perhaps Eusebios. (See also Cpt 2022)

Cpt_2066.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 18.1-11, 13-15 and 2 Corinthians 3.7-13, 14-4.2
Cpt_2066.c: Two papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 18.1-11, 13-15) and 2 Corinthians (frag 1: 3.7-13, 14-4.2 with pagination), and are from a codex with the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2067.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Christian amulet with some Greek formulae as well as Coptic prayers, invocations to Gabriel and Iao and 2 wing formations based on Ablanathanalba and Achramachamari.

Cpt_2068.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Probably a Christian amulet.

Cpt_2070.t: Papyrus fragment possibly from a letter
Cpt_2070.c: Papyrus fragment with Coptic text on both sides, possibly from a letter with the address on the back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2071.c: About 38 papyrus fragments with Coptic text on front and back, probably literary texts, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2072.c: Thirty-eight mostly blank papyrus fragments made in Egypt, possibly from fragmentary Coptic manuscripts in the collection.

Cpt_2073.t: Papyrus fragments from the Acts of Peter
Cpt_2073.c: Seven papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on both sides, preserving part of the story of Marcellus from the Acts of Peter, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Heb_752.c: Samaritan Pentateuch written on parchment by the copyist and liturgical hymn author Abisha ibn Pinhas ibn Joseph, dated 740 AH (1339-1340 AD), see folios 238-253. The text is arranged as a one-letter manuscript (with some instances of two-letter spacing), where justification was achieved by detaching a letter from the first and last words of each line. The manuscript retains notes from previous owners and deeds of sale on f.69: 23 Rajab 1308 AH (4 March 1891 AD), f.129: Jumada II 887 AH (July/August 1482 AD), f.169v: undated, two on f.227: Shawwal 844 AH (February/March 1441 AD) and 1308 AH (1890/1891 AD), and f.276v: 867 AH (1462/1463 AD). Signs of kissing are found on f.140v (Leviticus 9.22-10.1), f.179 (Numbers 6.21-23) and f.209v (Numbers 25.10).

Heb_753_1.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 4 bifolios (16 pages) containing Numbers 3.36–9.15, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_2.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 3 bifolios (12 pages) containing Exodus 2.21–7.26, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_3_1.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 26.7–27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' type manuscript, where justification was maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_753_3_2.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 31.13–32.1, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Separator dots or colons appear at the end of almost every line and some separation of the letters occurs to maintain justification but it is not consistent.

Heb_753_4.t: Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_4.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification is achieved by detaching the first letter of the first word and the last letter or two of the final word of each line.

Heb_753_5.t: Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_5.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Leviticus Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last letter from the final word of each line.

Heb_754.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Exodus 8.2-9.17, written on parchment, in the 15th or 16th century probably in Palestine, Syria or Israel. Vertical and horizontal guide lines were impressed on the page to assist the scribe. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where symmetry is maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_755.t: Deuteronomy 9.7–11.12 and 12.17–14.28 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_755.c: Three bifolios (12 pages) from a single quire of a Samaritan Pentateuch containing portions of Deuteronomy written in Samaritan majuscule on paper, and dated to the 14th–17th centuries. The central bifolio (4 pages) of the quire is missing. The first letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word on each line is separated for text justification.

Heb_761.c: Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century. The combination of historic water and insect damage has caused the spine area to 'block' together into sections, leaving much of the manuscript inaccessible for handling, display and digitisation. However, folios 335-353, which were in better condition, have been fully conserved and are accessible (see Heb 761.1).

Heb_761_1.c: Folios 335–353 from a Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century.

Heb_762.t: Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital
Heb_762.c: Manuscript containing a Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital (1542–1620), written in Hebrew in a rabbinic script in Damascus in the early 17th century. It contains 17 diagrams in gold, red and blue, with titles in gold. Two previous owners signed the first folio: Raphael Mosche Galico and Hayyim de Rosa, both Jewish kabbalists based in Damascus in the 18th century. Hayyim Vital was a prominent kabbalist and the chief disciple of Isaac Luria in Safed (Israel), whose teachings are primarily known through Vital’s compendium, Etz Hayyim (Tree of Life). This treatise is one of Vital’s own works.

Heb_763.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with Ashkenazi traits and tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The parchment is divided into 'pages' with folds at regular intervals. The beginning of the roll is scalloped and tapers to a point with attached leather strap, but is otherwise undecorated. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_764.c: Festival prayer book (Mahzor) written on parchment in Hebrew in an Italian square script and dated to the 14th or 15th century, with an illuminated frontispiece and Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout. The lower border of the frontispiece contains an unidentified coat of arms of a lion or rampant on a field of azure.

Heb_765.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script, probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The beginning of the sroll is rounded and the other end is attached to a wooden roller. Each 'page' or column of text is decorated with a border painted with an orange pigment. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_766.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_767.c: Large portion of a Sefer Torah on vellum containing Genesis to Exodus 39, written in Hebrew in an Ashkenazic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 19th century. It retains one wooden roller.

Heb_768.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The 'pages' or columns of text are divided by painted borders. Its silver case is housed separately (Heb 768.1). The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_768_1.t: Silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah)
Heb_768_1.c: Embossed silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah) probably made in Italy and dated to the 18th century. It is decorated with scroll work, floral design and an unidentified coat of arms ornamented with the 'hands of Cohen' and surmounted by a crown. The scroll was originally housed within the case, and when read was unfurled through the vertical slot then rerolled using the silver roller still attached to the scroll (see CBL Heb 768).

Heb_769.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The very beginning of the scroll is not preserved. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_770.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment (sheep skin) in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century, attached to a single wooden roller. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_771_1.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer and two verses from Exodus (column 1: Exodus 13.1-10; column 2: Exodus 13.11-14; column 3: Deut 6.4-9 (shema), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_2.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deuteronomy 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_3.c: Mezuza ('doorpost') on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deut 6.4-9 and 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment.

Heb_772.c: Illuminated Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) on vellum, written in an Italian square script in Italy and dated to the 14th or 15th century, ornamented with Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout and bound in a contemporary leather binding. Bookplate of a previous owner, Baron Horace de Landau (1824-1903), on lower cover paste-down.

Heb_773.c: Almost complete Sefer Torah on parchment containing Genesis 21:10 to the end, written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 17th or 18th century.

Heb_774.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Deuteronomy 9:13-33:19 written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script, and dated to the 17th century.

Heb_775_1.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 1.1-31.19, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_775_2.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 10.21-14.10, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_776_1.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Leviticus written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the second portion containing Numbers 21.9-29.19.

Heb_776_2.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Numbers 21.9-29.19 written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the first portion containing Leviticus.

Heb_777.c: Sefer Torah on parchment written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script in the 18th century.

Heb_778.c: A 19th-century book of remembrances or memorial book (Yizkor book) for the family of Judah ben Menahem. The title on the wooden cover says 'The Book of Life', a typical euphemism for a book commemorating the dead, with a crude carving of the tomb of Rachel. Ten members of the family are included, each with their name and date of death followed by longer Yizkor passages. Dates range from 1838 (Judah ben Menahem) to 1887 (Keyle Marcus). The illustration on f.1 is dated 1889.

Heb_779.t: Just measure (Kav ha-Yashar) and Orchard of pomegranates (Pardes Rimonim)
Heb_779.c: Paper folio with text written in Hebrew in an Oriental script, copied in the 18th or 19th century by a non-professional scribe in North Africa or the Middle East. The recto appears to be the title page for Kav ha-Yashar (Just measure) and a prayer from Pardes Rimonim (Orchard of pomegranates) is written on the verso. The title on the recto, ספר קב הישר (Sefer Kav ha-Yashar), is written beneath בשם רחמן (in the name of the Merciful One). Below this the scribe has written 'I am hereby beginning to write the Sefer Kav ha-Yashar, with the help of the Name (=God)', followed by a blessing on anyone who reads it (spelled incorrectly) and a curse on anyone who steals it. The drawing is probably a series of columns in emulation of contemporary printed-book title pages, with the beginning of the alphabet written in the damaged right-hand panel. Beneath the title for Kav ha-Yashar on the verso is a prayer from the Kabbalistic work Pardes Rimonim (An orchard of pomegranates).

Is_1401.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1401.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 20 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, with illuminated motifs (knots, stars, lobed medallions) as tenth verse counters throughout, sections from the Qur'an, suras 13:34 to 18:110 (but not continuous), probably Iraq, c. 800-900. Two other folios from this same dispersed manuscript are now in the Freer-Sackler museum in Washington, DC: F1929.72 and F1945.16.

Is_1405A.t: Two folios from the Blue Qur'an
Is_1405A.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1405A.c: Two folios from the Blue Qur'an. Codex, gold, silver and ink on indigo-coloured parchment, 2 folios in modern binding, Arabic text in black-outlined gold kufic script, with silver verse-markers within text and margin (fol. 1v), non-sequential text folios from the (dispersed) Blue Qur'an, Sura 2:60-65 (fol. 1) and Sura 2:93-101 (fol. 2), possibly Baghdad, Iraq (or Fustat, Egypt), undated, c. 775-850

Is_1405B.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1405B.c: Folio from the Blue Qur'an. Folio, gold, silver and ink on indigo-coloured parchment, Arabic text in black-outlined gold kufic script, silver verse-markers within text and margin (recto), from the (dispersed) Blue Qur'an, Sura 2:65-74, possibly Baghdad, Iraq (or Fustat, Egypt), undated, c. 775-850.

Is_1406.t: Illuminated folio, probably from a Qur'an
Is_1406.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1406.c: Illuminated folio, probably from a Qur'an. Single folio, colours and gold on parchment, horizontal panel of illumination, central roundel, eight-pointed star, and lightly-drawn backdrop of palmette-leaf trellis, with hasp ornament in the margin, possibly Syria or Iraq, c. 800-900

Is_1408.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1408.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, modern green silk-covered binding, 9 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, with sura heading (Sura 36, fol. 5v) in gold, and illuminated verse markers throughout, section from the Qur’an (Q35:33-36:17, missing one folio Q35:40-41), possibly from Juz'22 of a 30 volume set, unsigned, Iraq or Syria, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_1411.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1411.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. The sura headings of this Qur'an manuscript are written out in gold script, with a large and colourful palmette design projecting into the margin for extra emphasis. There is a full page of illumination at the start and conclusion of the text, each in a different design of interlocking circles (at the start) and checkerboard (at the end). The layout is typical for a multi-volume Qur'an of this date, each separate volume would have splendid illumination panels, usually on facing pages at the beginning and at the end of the book. However this manuscript does not contain a complete "thirtieth" (juz') or "sixtieth" (hizb) of the Qur'an's full text, and is therefore a fragment of the original volume. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 11 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, sura headings in gold with large illuminated palmette, illuminated frontispiece (1v), finispiece (11r) and text markers throughout, final section of the Qur'an (sura 92:2- sura 114

Is_1414.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1414.c: Miniature Qur'an. Very small format Qur'ans are easily carried, and have long been used to provide personal protection to their owners in times of need, such as war or sickness. This small codex measures 9.6 x 5.9 cm, with thirteen clearly-written lines per page. Two notes have been added by later owners, recording the birth of sons, in the years 1011 and 1022: was this Qur'an kept close during childbirth? Codex, ink, colour and gold on parchment, 21 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, partial text of juz' 29 of the Qur'an (sura 71:3 to 99:98), with later notes added (to the inner covers) recording the birth of a son in 1011 (4 Jumada 402H), and again in 1022 (16 Shawwal 413H), possibly Iraq, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_1417A.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1417A.c: Juz' 3 of the Khayqani Qur'an. The Khayqani Qur'an is an important early example of the Arabic script known as "New Style" (also called eastern kufic), which developed gradually in Qur'anic calligraphy away from the more angular kufic script. This multi-volume Qur'an has been dated to c. 900 because of a note added to Juz' 19: on the final page is a statement in Persian, signed by someone called Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani. He notes that he has checked the text and made corrections, signing and dating his comment to the month of Sha`ban 292H (June 905). There have been doubts about the authenticity of this extra note, but not about the manuscript itself. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 47 folios, Arabic text in New Style III (aka eastern kufic) script, illuminated verse-markers, Juz' 3 of the Qur'an (2:253 to 3:91), from a thirty-volume set, of which Juz' 19 (CB Is 1417D) has a note signed al-Khayqani and dated 292H (June 905), probably Iran, c. 900

Is_1417C.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an

Is_1417D.t: Juz' 18 and 19 of the Khayqani Qur'an
Is_1417D.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1417D.c: Juz' 18 and 19 of the Khayqani Qur'an. The Khayqani Qur'an is an important early example of the Arabic script known as "New Style" (also called eastern kufic), which developed gradually in Qur'anic calligraphy away from the more angular kufic script. This multi-volume Qur'an has been dated to c. 900 because of a note added to Juz' 19: on the final page is a statement in Persian, signed by someone called Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani. He notes that he has checked the text and made corrections, signing and dating his comment to the month of Sha`ban 292H (June 905). There have been doubts about the authenticity of this extra note, but not about the manuscript itself. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 46 folios, Arabic text in New Style III (aka eastern kufic) script, illuminated verse-markers, Juz' 18 and 19 of the Qur'an (25:1 to 27:55), from a thirty-volume set, of which Juz' 19 (fol. 46v) has a corrections note in Persian signed Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani and dated

Is_1421.t: Three Folios from Juz' 17 of the Qur'an
Is_1421.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1421.c: Three Folios from Juz' 17 of the Qur'an, donated to the Great Umayyad Mosque of Damascus in 911. These are the last folios from a Qur'an manuscript, that was part seventeen of a thirty-volume set. As the text ended, the artist added a double page of illumination to conclude the volume. The final page records that the full thirty-volume set was donated to the congregational mosque in Damascus in the month Dhu'l-Qa`da in 298H, the equivalent date for July 911. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 3 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, illuminated double finispiece (ff. 2v-3r), final verses of Juz' 17 of the Qur'an (sura 22:77-78), waqf notice (f. 3v) of donation in Dhu'l-Qa`da 298H (July 911) to the congregational mosque of Damascus, naming the donor `Abd al-Mun`im ibn Ahmad, Damascus, Syria, 911.

Is_1431.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1431.c: The Ibn al-Bawwab Qur’an was produced in Baghdad in the year 1000. Its smooth cursive calligraphy is the work of Abu’l Hasan `Ali ibn Hilal (d. 1022), more commonly known as Ibn al-Bawwab (meaning "son of the doorkeeper"). Ibn al-Bawwab is renowned as one of Islam’s greatest master-calligraphers, and this manuscript is held to be the only Qur’an genuinely written in his hand. It is also important for being one of the earliest dated Qur’ans copied on paper (as opposed to parchment) and one of the earliest written in a cursive script. In the year 1000, Baghdad was ruled nominally by the `Abbasid caliphs, who were in turn controlled by the Buyid dynasty. While this Qur'an is not documented as a royal commission, Ibn al-Bawwab had connections to the Buyid rulers: before coming to Baghdad, he had served as chief librarian for a Buyid amir's collection in Shiraz, Iran. Is_1437C.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1437C.c: Partial copy of Juz' 30 of a Mamluk Qur'an. This Qur'an is written out in tumar script, as opposed to the more fashionable Mamluk scripts thuluth or muhaqqaq. The calligrapher has been identified as Ibn al-Wahid (d. 1311), a renowned practitioner born in Damascus in 1249, who studied under Yaqut al-Musta`simi (d. 1298) in Baghdad and settled in Cairo. Together with the master-illuminator Sandal, Ibn al-Wahid worked on a monumental Qur'an project (today in the British Library) for the Mamluk Sultan Baybars in 1306, and they may also have worked together on this manuscript. Much is recorded of Ibn al-Wahid's biography (and personality), including that he worked in Sultan Baybars' chancery, where the secretary complained of his negligence. However he was greatly admired for his calligraphic skill by the forgiving Baybars. The unusual use here of tumar (normally a chancery script) may further support the manuscript's attribution to Ibn al-Wahid. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 116 f

Is_1448.c: Juz' 12 of the Sinjar Qur'an. Written out in gold thuluth script, this manuscript is from a thirty-volume set, now dispersed in worldwide collections. The twenty-eighth volume (in the Khalili Collection, London) includes a statement on the original commission: the set was produced in 1211 (607H), for the library of one of the last rulers of the Zangid dynasty Qutb al-Din Muhammad, in Sinjar (northern Iraq). Is_1457_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1457_1.c: Folio from a Mamluk Qur'an. This single folio belongs to a codex (also in this museum: Is 1457I and II). Each side is beautifully illuminated, and each was created as a double page design: the geometric star design on the recto (here) would have faced an identical folio, which is now lost. As often with Qur'ans from Mamluk Cairo, the white kufic inscriptions at the top and bottom are different Qur'anic quotations, referring to the holy book itself: "Indeed We have sent [the Qur'an] down in a Night of Blessings" (Qur'an 44:3, top), and "Indeed We have sent down [the Qur'an] in the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr)" (Qur'an 97:1, bottom). On the verso, different illumination frames the first sura of the Qur'an. This text should face the second sura of the Qur'an, with matching designs: that opposite page remains in the codex (CB Is 1457I). Is_1476.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1476.c: Qur'an from Mamluk Cairo. This manuscript contains Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, and it was originally one of a thirty-volume set of the complete text. The opening folios present an illuminated double page, with matching panels of radial geometric design. The central octagons read "The Twenty-Seventh Juz'", in angular white kufic script. Set against gold ground, four lines of smaller text frame these central panels, with a Qur'anic quotation: "Truly this [Qur'an] is a revelation, From the Lord of the worlds, Which the true Spirit has brought down upon your heart, That you may be one of the warners, In clear Arabic language" (Qur'an 26:192-5). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 48 folios, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script, with sura headings in thuluth, and illuminated double page frontispiece (fols. 1v-2r), Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, illumination and calligraphy attributed to Ahmad ibn Kamal ibn Yahya al-Ansari al-Mutatabbib (unsigned), Cairo, Egypt, c. 1332-1336.

Is_1500.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1500.c: Qur'an from Timurid Herat This magnificent copy of the Qur'an was produced at the Timurid court in Herat, almost certainly for Prince Baysunghur (d. 1433). The first page-opening is a double-page composition of illumination, with a radiating geometric star pattern. This deliberately echoes designs from the late thirteenth century, although the central lobed medallion is very much up to date for Timurid design. The Timurid calligrapher has also referred deliberately to the late thirteenth century, by signing in the name of the highly-regarded master-calligrapher Yaqut al-Musta`simi, who died in 1298. A very similar Qur'an was signed by the Timurid master-calligrapher Shams al-Baysunghuri, in 1434 (837H), and is today in the Turkish and Islamic Art Museum in Istanbul (TIEM 294). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 273 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, and angular kufic for first two sura headings, with initial double frontispiece of radial strapwork (fols. 1v-2r), complete Qur'an,

Is_1558.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1558.c: Qur'an, bound codex, 445 folios, ink, gold and pigments on paper, Arabic calligraphy and illumination, signed by Ruzbihan Muhammad al-Tab`i al-Shirazi (f.445r), Shiraz, Iran, c. 1535-1565. Produced in the city of Shiraz, this splendid Qur’an is an extraordinary example of the arts of the book in sixteenth-century Iran. The sacred text was written out by renowned master-calligrapher Ruzbihan. He used three different scripts to copy out the main text and further calligraphic styles for the chapter headings. Throughout the manuscript, the Qur'anic text is accompanied by a rich programme of sophisticated and colourful illumination, dominated by burnished gold and deep lapis blue.

Is_1614_1.c: Opening folio from a Qur'an, illuminated by Muhammad ibn Aybak in Baghdad. This full-page illumination marks the beginning of a superb Qur'an volume produced in Baghdad. It is from a thirty-volume set, now dispersed in international collections or lost. Four of the known volumes contain the signature of the renowned illuminator Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn `Abdullah, who also recorded the date and that he was working "in the City of Peace, Baghdad". From these inscriptions, Ibn Aybak's work schedule becomes clear: he completed volume two in April 1303, ten in February 1305, and thirteen in October 1305, producing an illuminated volume approximately every three months. Folio from a Qur'an, colours and gold on paper, illuminated frontispiece panel with geometric design of central radiating star with quarter-stars repeated in the four corners, and hasp ornament on right margin, right half of a double-page composition, illumination by Muhammad ibn Aybak, opening folio from volume 25 of a 30-volu

Four of the known volumes contain the signature of the renowned illuminator Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn `Abdullah, who also recorded the date and that he was working "in the City of Peace, Baghdad". From these inscriptions, Ibn Aybak's work schedule becomes clear: he completed volume two in April 1303, ten in February 1305, thirteen in October 1305, and volume twenty-six in 1306, producing an illuminated volume approximately every three months. Although his work does not figure in this particular folio, this Qur'an's calligrapher was also an important figure: Ibn al-Suhrawardi, trained by the great master Yaqut al-Musta`simi. Is_1615I.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1615I.c: Folios from a Hijazi Qur'an. Now placed in a modern binding, these Qur'an folios date from the first century of Islam, in either the Arabian peninsula or Syria. The Arabic is written in an unusual version of the script known as hijazi - meaning from Hijaz province, where the cities of Mecca and Medina are located. Codex, ink and colours on parchment, 32 folios, Arabic text in hijazi script, with illumination of horizontal chevron bands between chapters (suras), portion of the Qur'an (suras 28:6 to 48:24), unsigned, possibly Medina (modern Saudi Arabia) or Damascus (Syria), undated, c. 675-725.

Is_1615II.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1615II.c: Folios from a Hijazi Qur'an Now placed in a modern binding, these four Qur'an folios may date from the first century of Islam, in either the Arabian peninsula or Syria. The Arabic is written in an unusual version of the script known as hijazi - meaning from Hijaz province, where the cities of Mecca and Medina are located. Codex, ink and colours on parchment, 4 folios, Arabic text in hijazi script, with illumination of horizontal chevron bands between chapters (suras, on fol. 4v only), portion of the Qur'an (suras 85:3 to 110:1), unsigned, possibly Medina (modern Saudi Arabia) or Damascus (Syria), undated, c. 675-725.

Is_1622.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Handscroll; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1622.c: Qur'an scroll, with holy names in reserve. Written in minute ghubar script, this undated copy of the Qur'an shows a strong Shi`a conviction in its design, with the names of the Fourteen Immaculates reserved in large format throughout. This begins with the Prophet Muhammad and his daughter Fatima, followed by her husband `Ali ibn Abi Talib, and their male descendants. Similar scrolls reserve other Shi`a messages against the text of the Qur'an, such as the prayer to Imam `Ali ("Nad-e `Aliyan"). Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather flap cover, Arabic text in ghubar script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh) at the start, Qur'an with text reserved to form the sacred names of the Prophet Muhammad and his descendants (Fatima, `Ali, Hasan, Husayn, and all the other Shi`a Imams), Iran, undated, c. 1750-1850.

Is_1623.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1623.c: Qur'an scroll from Safavid Iran. Measuring over 6.7m in length, this paper scroll contains the entire text of the Qur'ān, written in a tiny script known as "ghubar" (dust). Also included - reserved against the tiny ghubar text - is a series of important prayers and invocations, addressed to the Prophet and his descendants through his daughter Fāṭima and her husband `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Together, they head a family line of altogether Twelve Imāms, who are of deep spiritual significance in Shi`a Islamic tradition. For this Qur'ān scroll, the special praise for the Twelve Imams fits with the cultural environment of Safavid Iran, which from 1501 was a Twelver Shi`a state. Scroll, ink, gold and colours on paper, Arabic text in ghubar script, with illuminated heading, the full text of the Qur'ān, with additional pious texts reserved against main text (the bismillāh, invocations to the Prophet, his daughter Fāṭima and the twelve Imāms (the Fourteen Innocents, or Chahārdah Ma`ṣūm), the prayer N

a: Muhammad ibn Mansur `Ali al-Hanafi al-Husayni al-Kakhtawi
Is_1624.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1624.c: Qur'an scroll from Mamluk Cairo. This remarkable Qur'an scroll is over 11m in length. It contains the complete text of the Qur'an, laid out in a sequence of shaped panels and also down the long borders on the sides, with gold-painted margins and leafy illumination throughout. There are also further sections, adding with the powerful primary blessing (baraka) associated with the Qur'an itself: a set of talismanic squares (awfaq) each linked with a different planet, followed by short prayers to the Prophet, the four Rashidun caliphs and Imams Hasan, Husayn and Ja`far al-Sadiq, all to protect the patron. This combination of Islamic faith with astrological concepts is a good example of "licit magic", a widespread social system of invoking protective unseen forces, used in conjunction with more mainstream religion. Is_1625.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1625.c: Qur'an scroll. Measuring over 11m in length and only 10cm in height, this scroll conveys the entire text of the Qur'an through a striking sequence of different calligraphic layouts, in which a large pious inscription dramatically overlays the packed and tiny text below. The outer borders meanwhile convey a long band of clearly written Qur'anic text (sura 112), written in gold. Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, backed on green silk, Arabic text in varying black, red, gold and white scripts (cursive and angular), periodically overlaying or reserving large thuluth, kufic or square kufic scripts against very small naskh or ghubar scripts, with illuminated sura-headings throughout, Qur'an (originally the complete text, suras 1, 2, 48 now missing), border naskh inscription repeating al-Ikhlas (sura 112), with panel grid of magic squares (awfaq), possibly Iran, undated, c. 1400-1450.

Is_1626.o: Scroll (object name); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1626.c: Qur'an scroll. Measuring over 7m in length, this narrow paper scroll contains the full text of the Qur'an, neatly written in tiny script. At the leather flap, the initial part of the scroll holds a series of Arabic inscription panels in banna'i script (also called square kufic), written here in black on white squared paper, but more commonly found in tiled architecture. Further banna'i inscriptions also line the border of the main text. Scroll, ink, colours and gold on paper, green cloth backing support, gold-painted leather flap with woven cotton band, Arabic text in naskh and banna'i (square kufic) scripts, with illuminated heading (sarlawh) and inscribed medallions, squares and stepped cartouches at the start, complete Qur'an, with additional prayers, possibly Shiraz, Iran, c. 1500-1600

Is_1627.t: Two Folios from a Mamluk Qur'an
Is_1627.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1627.c: Two Folios from a Mamluk Qur'an. These two folios were detached from a monumental Qur'an manuscript, probably in Paris in the late nineteenth century. Four of the six sura-headings (103, 104, 106, 109) do not belong to this page-opening: they have been cut out from other parts of the text, and pasted here over existing lines of text (suras 90-92). This can only have been to inflate the market value of these two folios, in a western context. The diversity of the illumination confirms what was once a splendidly produced Qur'an, with different artists working in distinct styles. Other folios from this same manuscript: CBL Is 1628, Boston Museum of Fine Arts 09.335, and Manchester John Rylands Ar.42 (the codex). Two folios, ink, colours and gold on paper, Arabic text in muhaqqaq, thuluth and kufic scripts, with six illuminated sura-headings and marginal motifs, final lines of sura 90 (al-`Asr) to sura 92 (al-Layl) of the Qur'an, and headings for suras 103, 91, 104, 106, 92, 109 respectivel

Is_1628.t: Closing folios from a Mamluk Qur'an
Is_1628.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1628.c: Closing folios from a Mamluk Qur'an. These two folios were the final page-opening of a monumental Qur'an made in Mamluk Cairo, possibly for Sultan al-Ashraf Sha`ban (r. 1363-76). A complex design of overlapping circles and white strapwork forms the framework for the final two sura titles (above), while the lower frame holds a separate quote ("And perfect are the words of your Lord..." Qur'an 6:115). In 1877, the French scholar Prisse d'Avennes published a colour drawing of a detail of this page-opening (fol. 2r, upper left) in his work on Arab art and design: he had seen the manuscript on display at the international exhibition in Paris, 1867. Other folios from this manuscript: CBL Is 1627, Boston Museum of Fine Arts 09.335, and Manchester John Rylands Ar.42 (the codex). Is_As44.c: Amulet, carnelian with incised text, Arabic text (around the borders) quoting the Throne Verse (Qur’an 2:255), and (in the centre) naming God, Muhammad and `Ali, Iran, 1676 (1087H)

Is_As51.t: Carnelian amulet carved with protective verses from the Qur'an
Is_As51.c: Amulet, carnelian, oval plaque with carved design, Arabic text in naskh script, four horizontal lines quoting the Qur’an (al-Nas, Sura 114:1-6), possibly India or Iran, undated, c. 1700-1900.

Is_As61.t: Amulet, with design of roses bearing holy names
Is_As61.c: Amulet, quartz with incised inscriptions design centred on a rosebush growing from a pot, labelled with holy names including the Fourteen Immaculates (the Prophet, his daughter Fatima and the Twelve Imams), and Qur'an verses (the Throne Verse 2:255, and al-Nas 112:1-4), Iran or India, 1656 (1067H).

Is_Pp1.t: Papyrus list of names and payments, written in Coptic
Is_Pp1.c: Papyrus list of names and payments, written in Coptic. This document is organised in two columns, consisting of personal names on the left followed by amounts on the right, using Greek letters as numerals. This relates to fiscal administration, recording land measures, tax payments or some other contribution imposed on the individuals listed in the first column. Some names and amounts are marked with an oblique stroke, as a tick or check mark. Some names are preceded by "ar" possibly an abbreviation of the content measurement unit "artabe" or the surface measurement unit "aroura", both of which fit the context of agricultural taxes. On the recto side, some names can be read, for example on column one: Mōne (line 1), George (line 2), Apollo (lines 3, 5), line 6 Ioannes de deacon (daikon, line 6), and on column two: George (line 8); Phib (line 9). Is_Pp2.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease dated Dhū al-Ḥijja 290H (October-November 903)
Is_Pp2.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease for the tax year 290H (903). This papyrus folio was used twice, first as a letter (on the verso side, written in the eighth century) and then for an agricultural legal contract in the year 903 (290H, on the recto). With papyrus breakage at the top and bottom of the folio (on the verso), some text is lost from both start and finish of the letter, but the surviving text begins with blessings wished on the addressee, and asks for a favour. Much of the detail is unclear: the sender requests politely that the addressee might undertake some task for their benefit, and mentions a third person who has passed on some information. On the recto of the papyrus folio the text is complete, and contains an agricultural lease (Ar. qabāla) dated to the month Dhu al-Hijja of the year 290H (October-November 903). The contract is issued by the tenant (mutaqabbil) Mīnā son of Qultah for grazing land (marj wa-marāʿ) on estates belonging to the amir in the town of Ṭuṭūn

Is_Pp3.t: Papyrus memo: tax evaders under arrest
Is_Pp3.c: Papyrus memo about tax evaders under arrest. This memo was issued from the administrative offices of the Arab authorities in Egypt, and deals with the topic of agricultural workers and land-owners who have left their place of fiscal residence and moved to another administrative district. Such "fugitives" (in Arabic s. jālī; pl jāliya) are mentioned in surviving papyrus documentation throughout Egypt’s history, but in the Islamic period they are especially prominent in the record from the end of the seventh and throughout the eighth century. The fugitives were treated variously depending on the circumstances: sometimes they had to pay taxes in their new place of residence, sometimes they had to pay taxes (as well) in their original place of residence while living and working elsewhere, and sometimes they were forced to return to their original place of residence to work the agricultural land and pay taxes there. Is_Pp4.t: Papyrus folios from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881)
Is_Pp4.c: Papyrus folios from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Two folio fragments, ink on dark brown papyrus, with (on left fragment) traces of the string which bound the original volume, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text in a practiced cursive hand with a thin pen, part of a surviving set of 3 bifolios and 1 single folio (CBL Is Pp4, 5 and 6), all fragments from the same original codex, Ḥadīth Traditions attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad on the benefits of prayer (du`ā’), compiled by Khayr, (right fragment: single folio) one half of the bifolio that originally formed the book’s cover, with title (verso) stating the author as Khayr, noting that Khayr obtained his text via his teacher Khālid ibn Yazīd in the year 267H (880-881), with three historical anecdotes perpendicular to the writing direction, added later, (left fragment: bifolio) middle part of the bifolio only, Egypt, dated 267H, 880-881.

Is_Pp5.t: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881)
Is_Pp5.c: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Bifolio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text in a practiced cursive hand with a thin pen, part of a surviving set of 3 bifolios and 1 single folio (CBL Is Pp4, 5 and 6), all fragments from the same original codex, Ḥadīth Traditions attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad on the benefits of prayer (du`ā’), compiled by Khayr, under supervision from his teacher Khālid ibn Yazīd, Egypt, dated (written in CBL Is Pp4) 267H, 880-881.

Is_Pp6.c: Papyrus bifolio from a Ḥadīth manuscript dated 267H (880-881). Is_Pp7.t: Papyrus pseudo-script, imitating a written letter
Is_Pp7.c: Papyrus pseudo-script, imitating a written letter. Folio fragment, ink on medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved on all sides, Arabic text written parallel to the fibres, basmala (line 1), followed by 17 lines of illegible writing in Arabic letter forms and X marks, possibly in magical or coded writing, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp8.t: Papyrus letter to `Abdullāh ibn As`ad in Fayyūm
Is_Pp8.c: Papyrus letter to `Abdullāh ibn As`ad: an unidentified request. `Abdullāh ibn As`ad is well-known as the administrator of a district south-west of al-Fayyūm, near the town of Narmūda (Gr. Narmouthis) in Egypt, in c. 730-750. This papyrus letter was therefore probably posted to him in al-Fayyūm, but where the letter was sent from remains an open question. The sender, `Amr b. `Abdullāh, is not otherwise known in the historical record. Extensive blessings and greetings take up most of the surviving part of this fragile papyrus letter, which strongly suggests its intended function as a polite letter of request. In the final line just before the papyrus breaks off, `Amr writes that he would like `Abdullāh to do something once he receives his letter: with the rest of the letter missing, it is impossible to know what exactly that amounted to. Folio fragment, ink on fine light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top, right and left sides

Is_Pp9.c: Papyrus accounts of the cloth merchant. Folio fragment, ink on medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved on the right and lower edges (recto) with some text loss at top and left, Arabic text, written in medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto) and parallel to the fibres (on verso), accounting sheet for a cloth merchant business, recording separate accounts (min al-ḥisāba), each with columns for (1:) lists of personal names, including identifiable Christian Egyptian (Coptic) and ethnic or professional nisba surnames, (2:) textile goods reckoned in robes, cloth and bales, and (3:) prices in dinars, qīrāṭs and fractions of ‘current’ coins (jawāz), or purses, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp10.c: Papyrus letter: an unidentified request. Folio fragment, ink on fine light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top and right edges, Arabic text, written with a medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto) and parallel to the fibres (on verso), (recto:) upper right corner of a letter to an un-named addressee, very politely expressed with extensive opening greetings, probably a request or petition, (verso:) written in the same hand, and probably a fragment of the letter's external address, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp11.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease: sowing wheat
Is_Pp11.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural lease . Folio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, broken off on all sides with text loss of text at top, left and right edges, Arabic text, written in a practiced cursive hand perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), and in a large hand with a thicker pen parallel to the fibres (on verso), two un-related documents, (recto:) agricultural lease (qabāla), witnessed document leasing one faddān of land for the cultivation of wheat, issued to Muḥammad son of `Abdullāh, (verso:) probably a letter, unsigned, Egypt, dated (on recto) between 271-279H or 291-299H, c. 884-911.

Is_Pp12.t: Papyrus letter and agricultural register: the wheat harvest
Is_Pp12.c: Papyrus letter and agricultural register: the wheat harvest. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, cut at the top and bottom for re-use, later broken on right side (recto), Arabic text, written with thin pen parallel to the fibres (on recto), and with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on verso), two un-related documents, (recto:) commercial letter confirming wheat deliveries and shipments, (verso:) agricultural register of crops sown, land used, wheat and trefoil harvest yield and resulting tax calculations owed by two land-holders, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 700-900.

Is_Pp13.t: Papyrus letters: goods delivery and the wheat crop
Is_Pp13.c: Papyrus letters about goods delivery and the wheat crop. Two folio fragments, ink on medium to light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thick pen perpendicular to the fibres, fragments of two letters, (Letter 1:) papyrus broken off at the top and right, with substantial loss of text, letter confirming the sender has dispatched "two bundles" of goods to the addressee, using Greek letters throughout as numbers, (Letter 2:) papyrus broken off at the top, bottom and right, letter refers to wheat, both documents unsigned, Egypt, undated, 800-900.

Is_Pp14.t: Papyrus tax receipt and payment register
Is_Pp14.c: Papyrus tax receipt and payment register. Folio fragment, ink on fine, light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, broken off on left edge (recto) with substantial text loss, Arabic text, written with a fine pen parallel to the fibres (on recto) and perpendicular to the fibres (on verso), (recto:) tax receipt for Muḥammad son of `Abdullāh, (verso:) six columns of figures, using Greek letters as numerals, for a register of payments or impositions presumably also linked to taxation, text on verso written first, after which the folio was re-used to write the recto text, unsigned, Egypt, dated (on recto) 241-249H, 855-863.

Is_Pp15.c: Papyrus letters: work and taxation. Folio fragment, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting line preserved on the left edge but broken off at the top (recto), Arabic text, written with a medium thick pen parallel to the fibres on recto, and a monumental script with a thick pen on verso, two separate letters about administrative work, (recto:) letter directing the addressee to perform a task, with reference to a paymaster (qusṭāl), (verso:) letter referring to taxation (al-kharāj), written in well-spaced chancery format, first used on the verso side then cut for re-use on the recto, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-1000.

Is_Pp16.c: Papyrus letters with agricultural discussions. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thick pen parallel to the fibres on recto, and in large well-spaced hand on the verso, two separate letters about agricultural work, (recto:) letter referring to plots of land for ploughing (ḥarth) or leaving fallow (fa-qad ʿaṭṭalat/ʿaṭṭaltu), and to other unnamed correspondents and messengers, (verso:) letter beginning and ending with polite blessings wished upon the (unnamed) addressee, first used on the verso side then cut for re-use on the recto, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp17.t: Papyrus letters in fragments: something happened
Is_Pp17.c: Papyrus letters in fragments: something happened. Fifteen folio fragments, ink on dark brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written with a thin pen perpendicular to the fibres on recto, and parallel to the fibres on verso, all fragments from the same single folio, two separate letters, (recto:) letter referring to something that happened “today” (fī hādhā al-yawm), and hoping that something else will happen God-willing (in shāʾa allāh), (verso:) letter referring to individuals (al-Ḥusayn, Muḥammad, Abū `Alī), unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_Pp18.t: Papyrus letter about finding a new tenant and selling a pearl in Fusṭāṭ, and a statement of accounts
Is_Pp18.c: Papyrus letter about finding a new tenant and selling a pearl in Fusṭāṭ, and a statement of accounts. Folio fragment, ink on light to medium brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic text, written perpendicular to the fibres, two separate documents, (on recto:) letter from a property-owner in Fayyūm asking a friend in Fusṭāṭ to get his estate agent Zayd ibn Muzāḥim to find a new tenant for a recently-vacated room with the rent set between 6 and 8 dinars a year, and then as a postscript, he asks the friend to follow up an expected payment of 16 dinars for a pearl that was recently sold by `Alā’ the jeweller, (on verso, added later:) list of accounts, in two columns, recording personal names and the money owed or received (in dirhams), unsigned, al-Fayyūm, Egypt, undated, c. 800-900

Is_Pp19.c: Papyrus ledger of accounts. Folio fragment, ink on light brown papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, original cutting lines preserved at top, left and right edges, broken at top and lower right, Arabic text written in two different hands, perpendicular to the fibres (recto) and parallel (on verso), folio from a fiscal ledger with account details presented in columns, with payments from different groups (including shepherds) due or completed in dinars, using Greek letters as numerals, unsigned, Egypt, undated, c. 700-900.

Is_Pp20.t: Six papyrus fragments of letters, lists and other documents
Is_Pp20.c: Six papyrus fragments of letters, lists and other documents. Six folio fragments, ink on papyrus, mounted on paper and framed under glass, Arabic and (for 53 only:) Coptic text, numbered 48 to 53 (stickers on glass frame), fragments from different documents, (48:) written on light papyrus with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), (recto:) list of names of men and women, followed by (verso:) columns of numbers in Greek letters, undated, 750-900, (49:) written on medium brown papyrus with thin pen parallel to the fibres (on recto), text repeats the bismillah, with possible pseudoscript, undated, 800-900, (50:) written on light brown papyrus with fine pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), fragment of a letter referring to money owed, undated, 700-900, (51:) written with medium thick pen perpendicular to the fibres (on recto), (recto:) fragment of a letter complaining about receiving threats, (verso:) receipt for payment of one dinar, with blessings wished on the addresse

Is_Pp21.c: Block-printed amulet on paper. Is_Pp22.c: Folio from the Prophet's biography. Is_Sc6.c: The astrolabe is an adjustable instrument that maps the stars, and has many other functions. The device can be set to the user’s location on earth, and to the correct time. On the front, the curling pointers on the openwork plate (al-`ankabut in Arabic, or spider) are each labelled with a star’s name. Invented in late classical times, the astrolabe was perfected in the early Islamic period. Astrolabe, brass, with incised text, mapping lines and decoration, instrument with six latitude plates, openwork rete (`ankabut), sight-rule (alidade), wedge (faras) and pin, engraved mapping lines and labels (throughout), dedicated to Safavid shah Sulṭān Ḥusayn (r. 1694-1722), produced and engraved (ṣana`ahu wa nammaqahu) by `Abd al-A’imma ibn `Abd al-Ḥusayn (signature and date on back), Isfahan, Iran, dated 1120H, 1708-1709.

Is_Tx2.t: Velvet panel for a balcony rail
Is_Tx2.c: Velvet panel for a balcony rail. This silk panel is designed to hang over a balcony rail, showing the same image on either side: a row of flowering plants, drafted with careful naturalism. While this reflects court taste in seventeenth-century India, the textile structure reveals that it was produced in contemporary Safavid Iran, almost certainly for export to neighbouring India. According to an inventory note on the back, by February 1648, the panel was in the royal textile store (farrashkhana) in Amer fort in Jaipur, then ruled by Maharaja Jai Singh I (r. 1621-1667). Panel, silk velvet, designed to hang over a balcony rail, two matching designs of leafy flowering plants and curling clouds against cream ground, bordered with floral scollwork of tulips and narcissi, on the reverse are five dated inventory statements written in Hindi in Devanagari script (ranging between 1648 and 1666), recording the textile's size and valuation, added at the royal textile store (farrashkhana) at Amer F

Is_X6.c: Book-stand (rahl). This book-stand folds out into a standing x-shape, to hold an open book. The functional design goes back many centuries, and is also produced in woodwork and other media. This one is very similar to another example (now in the V&A) produced by Mahomed Amin: his award-winning work was displayed at a 1903 exhibition in Delhi, celebrating the accession of Edward VII (r. 1901-1910) as Emperor of India. Folding book-stand (rahl), carved stone (bowenite, a variant of serpentine), with gold-overlaid steel frame, stonework probably Bhera, metalwork probably Sialkot, Pakistan, c. 1900.

Is_X17.c: Pair of doors with ivory inlay. These two doors contain a central design of carved ivory and wooden elements, which have been salvaged from an older pair (probably from a minbar, or pulpit), and re-mounted in modern frames. This type of composite reconstruction was an important woodworking industry in nineteeth-century Cairo, and represented a combination of fragment salvage and historicist imitation. The industry continued into the twentieth century. Few of the original decorative segments remain here, and the joiner has carved new "replacement" panels to fill up the geometric pattern. When closed together, the pair of doors create a single twelve-sided polygon in their central design. Two door (matching pair), wood frame with carved wood (unidentified) and ivory inlays, metal lock and hinges, each with main vertical panel of three half dodecagons (offset) with central radiating stars, smaller ivory-outlined panels at top and bottom, probably Cairo, Egypt, some of the carved ivory fol

Is_X33.c: Amulet case. Case, watered steel with gold inlay, hollow faceted cylinder with rounded ends and three loop attachments, designed to contain a paper scroll written with Islamic prayers, to protect the owner, Iran, c. 1750-1850.

Pap_1011.c: Christian amulet or magical text written in Greek on papyrus and made in Egypt probably in the 4th century. The horizontal breakage at regular intervals suggests the sheet was once folded or rolled. The amulet is composed of a serpent (or dragon) eating its own tail (οὐροβόρος) encircling an open bookroll filled with an eight-by-eight grid of Greek vowels. A bird at the top left holds a christogram (⳩) in its beak. The text on the serpent is a common magical palindrome, the final letters being ιαεω, the Greek magical rendering of the name Yaweh (with an additional letter). A tabula ansata (tablet with handles) hangs off the bottom of the serpent. The whole is surrounded by short names and phrases.

Per_104_1.t: Hushang kills the Black Div (recto) and Hushang discovers fire while killing a dragon with a stone (verso), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_104_1.c: Hushang kills the Black Div (recto) and Hushang discovers fire while killing a dragon with a stone (verso), folio from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) of Firdausi. Detached folio, ink, pigments and gold on paper, Persian text with three chapter-headings and two paintings, probably Tabriz, Iran, c. 1300. This folio is from a dispersed manuscript known to scholars as the "First Small Shahnama", of which seventy-seven folios are now in the Chester Beatty. The "Small Shahnama" manuscripts are the earliest known illustrated examples of the Book of Kings (Shahnama), the epic Persian poem composed c. 1010 by Firdausi. Two manuscripts are dispersed, and a third is in the Freer Gallery in Washington, DC. Of small format, these three manuscripts are undated, but usually attributed to c. 1300 on stylistic grounds. Details of iconography confirm that production was after the Mongol invasions of Iran and Iraq, and the establishment of Ilkhanid rule in 1258.

Dateable to the era of late Mongol Ilkhanid rule in Iran (the 1330s), a dramatic but fragmentary manuscript known as the Great Mongol Shahnama (and also as the Demotte Shahnama) is today dispersed across many international collections, including eleven folios in the Chester Beatty collection. Heavily worn, the manuscript was extensively restored in late nineteenth-century Tehran, probably at the Gulistan Palace library: the folios were trimmed, remargined, and renumbered, with missing text supplemented on new paper folios, written out by Tehran calligraphers following fourteenth-century style. Many of the paintings were retouched, with occasional Persian commentary written onto them (visible in this painting, Per 111.1). Dateable to the era of late Mongol Ilkhanid rule in Iran (the 1330s), a dramatic but fragmentary manuscript known as the Great Mongol Shahnama (and also as the Demotte Shahnama) is today dispersed across many international collections, including eleven folios in the Chester Beatty collection. Many of the paintings were retouched, with occasional Persian commentary written onto them (visible in this painting, Per 111.3). Per_113.c: Complete Works (Kulliyāt), by Sa'di. This is an early compilation of the complete works of the renowned Shiraz poet Sa`di. Spread across two illuminated pages (fols. 1v-2r), the table of contents is organised in two facing medallions, listing (anticlockwise) eight poetry book titles each, and a grid below, listing seven treatises. The manuscript text was never fully copied out, however, and stops after Kitab al-tarji`at (book of refrain poems). Codex, ink, colours, and gold on paper, 78 folios, Persian text in naskh script, illuminated contents list and headings, the Complete Works (Kulliyāt) of Sa'di (c. 1210-1292), introduction (added by a later compiler), double-page illuminated contents list (fols. 1v-2r) listing 23 works (seven treatises (risalat) and sixteen books (kitab), of which only eleven are present), possibly Shiraz, Iran, unsigned, undated, c. 1380

Per_118.t: Gushtasp kills a monster wolf, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama)
Per_118.c: Gushtasp kills a monster wolf, folio from the Book of Kings (Shahnama). While travelling incognito in Rum (the Roman Empire), the Iranian prince Gushtasp fights and finally kills a monster wolf with his sword. The wolf has already savaged Gushtasp's horse, so he has to continue fighting it on foot. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian verses in nasta`liq script, painting (on verso), detached folio from the Book of Kings (Shahnama), Iran, c. 1425-1450.

Per_119.t: Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di
Per_119.c: Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di. Codex, 48 folios, ink, pigments and gold on paper, eight paintings (all on detached folios), later leather binding, Persian text, nasta`liq calligraphy signed Ja`far al-Baysunghuri, dedicated to Timurid prince Baysunghur Mirza, Herat, Afghanistan, dated 830H, 1427. The radiating medallion (shamsa) on folio 1r announces that the book was produced on Baysunghur's orders, by his book treasury (khizanat al-kutub) - referring the court workshop of artists. Sa`di (d.1290) of Shiraz is one of Iran's greatest classical poets. Pithy as well as ethical, the distinctive lines of the Rose Garden (Gulistan) combine prose tales (hikayat) with inserted poetry (bayt), and have been admired for centuries. This beautiful illustrated manuscript was produced in Herat, at the court of the Timurid prince Baysunghur (d. 1433), a renowned book-lover, art patron and bon vivant. Per_119_3.t: The poet with his friends in the orchard at night, from Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di
Per_119_3.c: The poet with his friends in the orchard at night, from Prince Baysunghur’s Rose Garden (Gulistan). The prologue of the Gulistan tells how one night the middle-aged poet was feeling anxious about his life's achievements so far, when his friend called in and began to cheer him up. They went out, and sat in another friend's orchard, enjoying the spring flowers and the night air. Heading home at dawn, Sa`di resolved (to his friend's delight) that he would write a book called the Rose Garden (Gulistan), with chapters on friendship, good conversation, happiness, youth and age, education, kingship and piety. Per_119_9.c: The king takes pity on the beggar, from Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di. Drinking late at night, a king sent a purse of cash and new clothing to a beggar outside his palace. The following day, the king was irritated to learn that the beggar had returned, having spent the money and sold the robe. His minister calmed him down, advising instead to provide the man with a smaller but regular allowance. Per_119_32.c: The robber-chief changes his opinion of the poet, from Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di. A poet tried to impress a robber-chief by composing a praise poem about him. Instead the chief had him stripped and threw him out. As the village dogs came to attack him, the poet tried in vain to dislodge some frozen stones from the ground, and he swore angrily about a village where the stones were fixed but the dogs were loose. The robber chief overhead this, and was highly amused. He returned the poet's clothes, and rewarded him with money and a new coat. Per_119_36.c: A lady offers a cool drink to the poet, from Prince Baysunghur's Rose Garden (Gulistan) by Sa`di. The poet recalled an extremely hot day in his youth, when he was walking down a street at noon, thirsty and weak. A beautiful woman came out of a house, and handed him an iced drink. Refreshed from his physical thirst, he found himself longing instead for the kind stranger. Per_120.t: Frontispiece from Prince Baysunghur's Anthology of Wise Sayings
Per_120.c: Frontispiece from Prince Baysunghur's Anthology of Wise Sayings. The golden calligraphy at the heart of this elaborate composition describes the main text to follow, a collection of "fine and rare phrases" and "pearls and jewels of ideas", compiled on the orders of Timurid prince Baysunghur (d. 1433), a celebrated book-lover and art patron. Unfortunately the first two pages (CBL Per 120.1 and Per 120.2) are all that now remains. Detached folio, pigments and gold on gold-flecked paper, re-mounted later, Arabic text in thuluth and kufic scripts, ogival medallion with cartouche below, framed within illuminated borders, one half of a double-page composition, frontispiece from an otherwise lost manuscript dedicated to Timurid prince Baysunghur, Herat, Afghanistan, c. 1430.

Per_127_95.t: Rustam captured by the Akvan Div, extract from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi, in Anthology of Ghazals (Ghazaliyyat al-motafarriqeh) by multiple authors
Per_127_95.c: Rustam captured by the Akvan Div, extract from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi, in Anthology of Ghazals (Ghazaliyyat al-motafarriqeh) by multiple authors. This painting depicts an episode in Firdausi's Book of Kings, in which the great hero Rustam has been kidnapped while sleeping, by the evil demon known as the Akvan Div. The demon has lifted away the ground beneath the sleeping hero, in order not to wake him up. The demon hovers above the earth, and asks Rustam to choose his death - would he prefer to be thrown to the rocks below or into the sea? Knowing that the Akvan Div will do the reverse, Rustam asks to be thrown to the land, and is therefore hurled down into the waves. He swims ashore, and escapes. Per_144_1.t: Introductory medallion (shamsa), from Bal`ami's History (Tarikh-i Bal`ami)
Per_144_1.c: Illuminated medallion (shamsa), from Bal`ami's History (Tarikh-i Bal`ami). This complex radiating design has a matching twin on the opposite page. Seen together, the pair of medallions occupy the book's first page-opening, and introduce a magnificent manuscript produced in Timurid Herat (Afghanistan). Formed of four radially-symmetrical quarters, each circular design features two layers of scrolling plant stems, painted in gold and jade green, against a deep blue ground. The medallion on the right has been salvaged from a slightly earlier manuscript, and has been pasted very subtly onto this page. The medallion on the left is a careful copy, made in 1470, along with the rest of this manuscript. Per_144_2.c: Medallion (shamsa) and text with illuminated borders, from the History by Bal`ami (Tarikh-i Bal`ami). This illuminated medallion marks the first page-opening of this magnificent book, and the text itself begins overleaf, framed within an illuminated border. The medallion on the right has been salvaged from a slightly earlier manuscript, and has been pasted very subtly onto this page. The medallion on the left (shown here) is therefore a careful copy, made in 1470, along with the rest of this manuscript.
