Per_144_20.t: Jamshid teaches the crafts to humanity, from Bal`ami's History (Ta'rikh-i Bal`ami)
Per_144_20.c: Jamshid teaches the crafts to humanity, folio from Bal`ami's History (Ta'rikh-i Bal`ami). This account of ancient kings and prophets describes here the reign of Jamshid, a legendary ancient king of Iran, whose benevolent reign was peaceful and productive. Jamshid introduced to humanity many of the craft technologies, including spinning, weaving, needlework and tailoring, and metalworking (all illustrated here). Writing in late tenth century Bukhara at the Samanid court of Mansur ibn Nuh (r. 961-976), the minister and historian Muhammad al-Bal`ami composed a new work in Persian, translating and supplementing The History of the Prophets and Kings (Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk, in Arabic) by the `Abbasid scholar Abu Ja`far Muhammad al-Tabari (d. 923). This illustrated copy of Bal`ami's history was produced in Timurid Herat, in the year 1470. Per_149.t: Collection (majmū`a) of Persian poetry, by Amīr Ḥusaynī (d. 1318), Awḥadī Marāgha’ī (d. 1338) and Salmān Sāvajī (d. 1376)
Per_149.c: Collection (majmū`a) of Persian poetry, by Amīr Ḥusaynī (d. 1318), Awḥadī Marāgha’ī (d. 1338) and Salmān Sāvajī (d. 1376) This manuscript was originally to contain five Persian poems, as listed in the illuminated rosette on the first page. Three poems now remain, composed by different poets of the fourteenth century, all in the fashionable romantic genre of "Dah-nāma" (Ten Letters) in which lovers communicate only via letter. There are six illustrations, on folios now detached from the codex, also in the Chester Beatty Persian collection (CBL Per 149.4, Per 149.24, Per 149.39, Per 149.58, Per 149.78, Per 149.96). The manuscript has been rearranged more than once: the first page is dedicated to prince Abū Sa`īd (r. 1451-69), who ruled the diminishing Timurid empire from Herat. A century later, the anthology was mounted in new gold-painted borders, at the Shaybanid court in Bukhara. Per_149_4.t: The lonely poet, from Thirty Letters (Sī-nāma, or Love Letters, `Ishq-nāma) by Amīr Ḥusaynī (d. 1318)
Per_149_4.c: The lonely poet, from Thirty Letters (Sī-nāma, or Love Letters, `Ishq-nāma) by Amīr Ḥusaynī (d. 1318). This poem is about lovers writing to each other when they are apart, and waiting to read each other’s letters. Here the thoughtful poet sits alone in his bedroom, on a starry night. Two books lie beside him, his reed pen ready in the white inkpot. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, re-mounted in gold-painted borders, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto), from Thirty Letters (Sī-nāma, also called Love Letters, `Ishq-nāma) by Amīr Ḥusaynī Fakhr al-Sādāt (d. 1318, Herat), from a collection (majmū`a) of Persian poetry, dedicated to Timurid ruler Abū Sa`īd (r. 1451-69), decorated borders added later by order of Shaybanid ruler `Abd al-Azīz (r. 1540-1549), probably produced in Herat, Afghanistan, c. 1450, with borders added in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, c. 1540-1549.

Per_149_24.c: The poet takes a cup of wine, from Thirty Letters (Sī-nāma, or Love Letters, `Ishq-nāma) by Amīr Ḥusaynī (d. 1318). Per_149_58.c: The lover reads his letter delivered by the older woman, from Ten Letters (Dah-nāma) by Awḥadī Marāgha’ī (d. 1338) The young man sits beside the older woman in the courtyard, eagerly reading the letter she has just brought him from his beloved. Per_149_96.c: The lovesick king conversing with the bird at night, from the Book of Separation (Firāq-nāma) by Salmān Sāvajī (d. 1376). a: Mir Shaykh Muhammad ibn Shaykh Ahmad
Per_156_9.c: The pious man riding a panther, from the Garden (Bustan) of Sa'di. A man stares in astonishment to see someone riding through the landscape on a wild panther, holding a snake in one hand. Sa`di tells this anecdote about a particularly pious individual, who has achieved such willing submission to God, that all dangerous creatures have submitted willingly to him. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, later re-margined, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from the Garden (Būstān) of Sa`di, folio detached from the codex (CB Per 156) signed by Mir Shaykh Muhammad ibn Shaykh Ahmad, dated Shawwal 883H, January 1479, but probably later.

Per_157_9.t: Gayumars enthroned, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
a: Unknown; Muhammad Baqqal; Abu al-Qasim Firdausi
Per_157_9.c: Gayumars enthroned, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Firdausi's epic Book of Kings was composed c. 1010, and tells in Persian verse the mythical histories of fifty kings and queens from ancient pre-Islamic Iran. The stories blend historical figures and events with dramatic legend, featuring superhuman heroes, supernatural monsters and kings of variable quality. Depicted here is Gayumars, the first king at the dawn of time. He and his people live in the mountains, where Firdausi writes that all dress in leopard skin, and live in peace. Detached folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian poetry in nasta`liq script, caption in gold ("the reign of Gayumars was for thirty years"), painting (on recto), text copied by Muhammad Baqqal, Shiraz, Iran, dated 23 Jumada I 885H, 1480

Per_157_11.c: Jamshid teaches the crafts, folio from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Firdausi's epic Book of Kings was composed c. 1010, and tells in Persian verse the mythical histories of fifty kings and queens from ancient pre-Islamic Iran. The stories blend historical figures and events with dramatic legend, featuring superhuman heroes, supernatural monsters and kings of variable quality. Depicted here is Jamshid, a splendid king whose rule introduces the crafts to mankind, as well as agriculture, architecture, mining and medicine. Per_157_81.t: Kay Kavus attempts to fly, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
a: Unknown; Muhammad Baqqal; Abu al-Qasim Firdausi
Per_157_81.c: Kay Kavus attempts to fly, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Firdausi's epic Book of Kings was composed c. 1010, and tells in Persian verse the mythical histories of fifty kings and queens from ancient pre-Islamic Iran. The stories blend historical figures and events with dramatic legend, featuring superhuman heroes, supernatural monsters and kings of variable quality. Depicted here is the unwise Kay Kavus, a king who makes several poor decisions throughout his reign, to the despair of his nobles. Tempted to fly, he orders a contraption built with four tame eagles strapped to it, and takes off in it. The flying throne works for a short time, but the king eventually crashes unhurt in the remote countryside. Detached folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian poetry in nasta`liq script, painting (on verso), text copied by Muhammad Baqqal, dated 23 Jumada I 885H, Shiraz, Iran, 31 July 1480

Per_157_370.t: Iskandar visits the Ka‘ba in Mecca, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
a: Unknown; Muhammad Baqqal; Abu al-Qasim Firdausi
Per_157_370.c: Iskandar visits the Ka‘ba in Mecca, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Firdausi's epic Book of Kings was composed c. 1010, and tells in Persian verse the mythical histories of fifty kings and queens from ancient pre-Islamic Iran. The stories blend historical figures and events with dramatic legend, featuring superhuman heroes, supernatural monsters and kings of variable quality. Depicted here is an episode from the reign of Iskandar, or Alexander the Great. Firdausi describes how Iskandar conquers Iran and India, and then pauses to make a pilgrimage to the Ka`ba shrine in Mecca, before proceeding to Egypt. In Mecca he meets the descendants of the prophet Ibhraim (Abraham). Detached folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian poetry in nasta`liq script, caption in gold ("Iskandar goes to the Ka`ba") and painting (on recto), text copied by Muhammad Baqqal, dated 23 Jumada I 885H, Shiraz, Iran, 31 July 1480.

Per_162_73.t: Shīrīn visits the sculptor Farhād as he works, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī (d. 1209)
Per_162_73.c: Shīrīn visits the sculptor Farhād as he works, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī (d. 1209). The Armenian princess Shirin hired the great engineer Farhad to carve a channel through the mountains, to bring the milk from her herds directly to her new palace. Having completed this incredible task, Farhad also carved an image of the beautiful princess into the purple rockface: he had fallen deeply in love with Shirin. Sadly for Farhad, Shirin was devoted only to king Khusrau of Iran. In this moment, the princess visits Farhad as he works. He pauses his carving and gratefully accepts the drink she offers him. The rock carving painted here is based on a real monumental relief from Taq-e Bustan in Iran, built for the pre-Islamic Sasanian king Khusrau II (r. 590-628). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting and illuminated caption (on recto), from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī (d. 1209), text copied by Murshid (signed colophon in codex, Pe

Per_163_6.t: Sufis performing samā` before their master Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyā (d. 1325), from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Amīr Khusrau (d. 1325)
Per_163_6.c: Sufis performing samā` before their master Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyā (d. 1325), from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Amīr Khusrau (d. 1325). These Sufis are performing the mystical ritual of samā`,in which the group combines music and movement with spiritual remembrance of God. Seated on a carpet at the head of the room, their master Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyā (d. 1325) observes the group. He was (and remains) a revered leader of the Chishtiyya Sufi order in India. The poet Amīr Khusrau (the composer of this poem), was also one of Shaykh Nizam al-Din’s followers, and is buried at his tomb in Delhi. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto), from the Rising Lights (Maṭla` al-anvār), from codex (CB Per 163) of the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Amīr Khusrau (d. 1325), copied by Muḥammad ibn Aẓhar, Herat, Afghanistan, dated 1 Rajab 890H, 14 July 1485.

Per_175.t: Book of the constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita), by `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986), in Persian translation
Per_175.c: Book of the constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita), by `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986), in Persian translation. This manuscript is Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī's Persian translation of the well-known Arabic treatise, the Book of the Constellations, by the Iranian astronomer `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986). Al-Ṣūfī's book is organised into forty-eight chapters, one per constellation. Each constellation is discussed and illustrated, and its constituent stars are catalogued in a table recording positions in celestial longitude and latitude (for the year 964). In this manuscript, the constellations are shown first as labelled dots, with no figure drawn around the stars, and then again as fully illustrated figures. The manuscript may have been copied from an un-illustrated work, but its owner wished to add the constellation figures which are usually part of al-Ṣūfī's treatise. Per_182_44.t: Khusrau sees Shīrīn bathing, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_44.c: Khusrau sees Shīrīn bathing, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The second poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the story of Khusrau and Shīrīn (Khusrau va Shīrīn), which describes the long and complicated romance between the Iranian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shīrīn. An embarrassing encounter happened early in their relationship. Until this moment, the two had never met in person. Shīrīn had fallen in love with Khusrau after seeing his portrait. He in turn had only heard about Shīrīn’s great beauty. Both rode out from their distant kingdoms to meet at last. Their paths crossed at the precise moment when Shīrīn had paused for a refreshing bath in a mountain pool. Their eyes met but they did not recognise each other. He rode on. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from Khusrau va Shīrīn, in the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī Ganjavī (d. 1209), Iran, text copied by `Alī al-Kātib (final colophon in codex Per 182, fol. 33

Per_182_51.t: Khusrau kills a lion outside Shīrīn’s tent, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_51.c: Khusrau kills a lion outside Shīrīn’s tent, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The second poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the story of Khusrau and Shīrīn (Khusrau va Shīrīn), which describes the long and complicated romance between the Iranian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shīrīn. After various delays, Khusrau and Shirin finally met in person at the court of Shirin’s aunt, the Queen of Armenia. As they got to know each other, the couple spent time hunting during the day, and celebrating in the evening. Each night the royal entourage set up their tents in the wilderness, and Khusrau and Shirin feast together under the stars. One night a dangerous lion came to the encampment. Unarmed, Khusrau fought it off with his bare hands. Per_182_69.t: The sculptor Farhād receives a drink from Shīrīn, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_69.c: The sculptor Farhād receives a drink from Shīrīn, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The second poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the story of Khusrau and Shīrīn (Khusrau va Shīrīn), which describes the long and complicated romance between the Iranian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shīrīn. Their relationship foundered when, to save his political career, Khusrau married another princess and Shīrīn was left alone. Full of sorrow, she moved to a remote region. Planning some complex technical improvements at her new home, Shīrīn hired the expert sculptor and engineer, Farhād. Completing the work, he fell hopelessly in love with Shīrīn. Now jealous, Khusrau ordered the sculptor to carve a roadway through a massive mountain. As Farhād worked, Shīrīn brought him a drink of milk, which he drank down in one gulp. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting and framed rubric (on recto), from Khusrau va Shīrīn, in the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī

Per_182_95.t: Shīrīn mourning the murdered Khusrau, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_95.c: Shīrīn mourning the murdered Khusrau, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The second poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the story of Khusrau and Shīrīn (Khusrau va Shīrīn), which describes the long and complicated romance between the Iranian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shīrīn. After much drama, the couple finally did get married, and lived happily together. Their joy ended with the jealousy of Khusrau’s son from his previous marriage. Attacking the palace, the younger man seized the throne from his father, and demanded that Shīrīn marry him instead. She refused, and both Khusrau and Shīrīn were imprisoned. Overnight, an assassin stole in and killed Khusrau as the couple slept. Shīrīn was heartbroken, and immediately planned her own death. Per_182_182.t: The Fairy Queen Turktāz welcomes Turktāzī to her magical court, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_182.c: The Fairy Queen Turktāz welcomes Turktāzī to her magical court, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The fourth poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is titled the Seven Beauties (Haft Paykar). This is a set of seven fantasy tales, told to the Iranian king Bahrām Gūr. The king had married seven princesses from around the world, and visited each one on a different night of the week. On Saturday he visited his Indian wife, and she told him the following story. A man found a magical way to visit an all-female court of beautiful fairies. Sadly, his rising hopes for romance with the Fairy Queen herself were abruptly disappointed. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from the Seven Beauties (Haft Paykar), in the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī Ganjavī (d. 1209), Iran, text copied by `Alī al-Kātib (final colophon in codex Per 182, fol. 331v), dated (codex Per 182, fol. 29v) Shawwal 915H, January 1510, painting c. 1550.

Per_182_256.t: Iskandar relaxes with Queen Nūshāba of Barda’, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_256.c: Iskandar relaxes with Queen Nūshāba of Barda’, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The fifth poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the Book of Alexander (Iskandar nāma), which describes the life and career of the historic Alexander of Macedon (d. 323 BC), called Iskandar in Persian literary tradition. The first section follows his conquests across Eurasia. Towards the end, he formed a new alliance with the wise Azeri queen Nūshāba, at the time of the spring equinox and the Persian New Year (Nawrūz). In celebration, Iskandar held a banquet in Nūshāba’s honour, outside in the spring sunshine. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and framed rubric (on verso), from Book of Alexander (Iskandarnāma), in the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī Ganjavī (d. 1209), Iran, text copied by `Alī al-Kātib (final colophon in codex Per 182, fol. 331v), dated (codex Per 182, fol. 29v) Shawwal 915H, January 1510, painting c. 1550.

Per_182_311.t: Iskandar learns he has been accepted by God as a prophet, on his deathbed, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī
Per_182_311.c: Iskandar learns he has been accepted by God as a prophet, on his deathbed, from the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī. The fifth poem in Niẓāmī’s Khamsa is the Book of Alexander (Iskandar nāma), which describes the life and career of the historic Alexander of Macedon (d. 323 BC), called Iskandar in Persian literary tradition. In the second section, Iskandar turned away from world conquest, and worked to develop wisdom and a better understanding of life. He met with philosophers to discuss these deeper ideas. Finally Iskandar reached a more spiritual sense of reality, and devoted himself to God. Here a divine messenger comes to Iskandar’s deathbed, to tell him God has accepted him as a Prophet. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with framed rubric (on recto) and painting (on verso), from the Book of Alexander (Iskandarnāma), in the Five Poems (Khamsa) by Niẓāmī Ganjavī (d. 1209), Iran, text copied by `Alī al-Kātib (final colophon in codex Per 182, fol.

Per_188_77.t: The beggar at the mosque doorway, from the Garden (Būstān) by Sa`di (d. 1292)
Per_188_77.c: The beggar at the mosque doorway, from the Garden (Būstān) by Sa`di (d. 1292). This scene shows the busy environment of a well-endowed mosque complex in the early sixteenth century, with working staff including a teacher who instructs two well-dressed young men inside. Standing by the doorway on the lower left, an elderly man waits patiently for generosity from a passerby. Under the mosque dome is a line of text quoting the poet Awḥadi (d. 1338). Folio, ink, colours and gold on gold-flecked paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated text panels and rubrics (on recto) and painting (on verso), from codex (CBL Per 188) the Garden (Būstān) by Sa`di (d. 1292), probably Herat, Afghanistan with painting added later in Ottoman Turkey, undated, c. 1490, additions c. 1525.

Per_192.t: Revelations of the two Holy Sanctuaries (Futūḥ al-Ḥaramayn), by Muḥyī al-dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Lārī (d. 1527)
Per_192.c: Revelations of the two Holy Sanctuaries (Futūḥ al-Ḥaramayn), by Muḥyī al-dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Lārī (d. 1527). Composed in Gujarat (India) and written in Persian, this poem describes the holy Islamic sites of Mecca and Medina, where the Hajj pilgrimage takes place every year. Painted in bright colours, the diagrammatic maps illustrate seventeen different locations for the Hajj ritual, including the Ka`ba sanctuary in Mecca. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, blind-tooled leather covers, 64 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (fol. 1v, sarlawh), and 17 painted maps and diagrams throughout, Revelations of the two Holy Sanctuaries (Futūḥ al-Ḥaramayn), by Muḥyī al-dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Lārī al-Anṣārī (d. 1527), poetic description of the Hajj pilgrimage routes and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina, original text dedicated to Muẓaffar Shāh II of Gujarat (r. 1511-1526), unsigned, possibly Iran or India, undated, c. 1525-1550.

Per_212_32.t: The planet Jupiter as a scholar, from a Persian cosmology treatise
Per_212_32.c: The planet Jupiter as a scholar, from a Persian cosmology treatise. This folio is from a wide-ranging book on cosmology, outlining recorded knowledge of the skies and the earth, and describing natural wonders. Discussed here are the planet Jupiter’s earthly (or "natural") influences, affecting world regions, human behaviours, and the wider natural and mineral worlds. In Middle Eastern scientific imagery, Jupiter is depicted as a senior scholar. Here he sits cross-legged, holding up a pen. Books are stacked on a folding book-stand beside him, with an hour-glass in between. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, heading (Jupiter, or Mushtari) in blue, with painting (on verso), from cosmology treatise composed in fifteenth-century Shiraz, adapted and expanded from Zakariya al-Qazvini's Wonders of Creation in Persian translation, text copied by Murshid al-Katib al-Shirazi known as `Attar, Shiraz, Iran, dated 25 Jumada I 952H, 4 August 1545. Per_224_7.t: Nūshīrvān listens to the owls, from the Treasury of Secrets (Makhzan al-asrār) by Niẓāmī
Per_224_7.c: Nūshīrvān listens to the owls, from the Treasury of Secrets (Makhzan al-asrār) by Niẓāmī. The poet Niẓāmī tells how the young king Nūshīrvān was out riding with his wise minister, on a hunting trip. Separated from the others, the two paused at a ruined village. Hearing two owls hooting in the ruins, the king asked the older man what he thought the birds were saying. The minister took the opportunity to give some delicate political advice: the owls were talking about the king himself, he explained, and how his terrible government policies were ruining so many villages throughout the land. This was good news for owls, who were masters of all derelict buildings. Shocked by the truth of this lesson, Nūshīrvān got the point, and promised to improve right away. The artist has added graffiti to the crumbling walls on the upper left of this painting. These lines are more quotations from Persian poetry, all addressed to owls. Per_225_1.t: Calligraphy in Arabic and Persian, folio from an album for Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
Per_225_1.c: Calligraphy in Arabic and Persian, folio from an album for Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah. This folio contains two samples of fine calligraphy, written by renowned masters Malik Daylami and his student Mir `Imad al-Hasani (d. 1615). It was once part of a calligraphic poetry album, produced for Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, who ruled the Deccani sultanate of Golconda. Some of the sultan's own poetry (beautifully written out by his court calligraphers) is included in the compilation, as well as older examples of fine calligraphy from Iran (such as these), and a tinted drawing. There are at least fifteen known folios from this album, which was re-bordered at a late date. Album-page, ink, gold and colours on paper, mounted on card, Arabic lines in nasta`liq script praising the Prophet Muhammad, signed `Imad al-Hasani (recto) and Persian verses praising a king, signed Malik Daylami in Nakhchivan, dated 961H, 1554 (verso), folio from an album compiled for Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (r. 1580-1612), Golconda

Album-page, ink, gold and colours on paper, mounted on card, Dakhni verses about Shab-i Barat (15 Sha`ban, Night of Forgiveness, also 12th Imam's birthday), signed Muhammad Reza, undated (recto), Dakhni verses about the end of `Id Ramadan, signed Muhammad Reza, undated (verso), folio from an album compiled for Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (r. 1580-1612), Golconda and Hyderabad, Deccan, India, c. 1590-1605.

Per_227.c: Forty Traditions (Arba`ūn Ḥadīth), by Jāmī. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 9 folios, Arabic and Persian text in nasta`liq script, illuminated shamsas with owner's seal impression (fols. 1r, 9v), illuminated heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v), and tinted drawing (fol. 2r, inserted seventeenth century), gold-flecked marbled borders throughout, Forty Traditions (Arba`ūn Ḥadīth), Arabic text in larger script followed by Persian paraphrase and commentary, composed 1481 by `Abd al-Raḥmān Nūr al-Dīn Jāmī (1414-1492), copied by Shah Mahmud Nishapuri, Mashhad, Iran, dated 964H, 1557.

Per_231.t: Stories of the Prophets (Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyā), by Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Nīshāpūrī
Per_231.c: Stories of the Prophets (Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyā), by Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Nīshāpūrī. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 284 folios, Persian text in black nasta`liq script, with occasional Arabic text in gold naskh script, with illuminated medallions (shamsas, fols. 1v-2r) and double page frontispiece (fols. 2v-3r), and 25 paintings (fols. 13v, 18v, 22r, 25r, 29v, 31r, 37r, 53v, 59v, 67v, 107v, 134r, 156r, 161v, 180r, 188v, 191v, 202r, 205v, 220r, 242v, 253r, 261v, 271r, 275r), Stories of the Prophets (Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyā), by Ibrāhīm ibn Manṣūr ibn Khalaf al-Nīshāpūrī, biographies of the Prophets and early Caliphs, unsigned, possibly Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1570-1590.

Per_231_227.t: Maryam (Mary) at the palm tree with baby `Isa (Jesus), from Stories of the Prophets (Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyā), by Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Nishapuri.
Per_231_227.c: Maryam (Mary) at the palm tree with baby `Isa (Jesus), from Stories of the Prophets (Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyā), by Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Nishapuri. This work describes the biographies of the Prophets in Islam, in chronological order from Adam to Muhammad. Many of these figure in the Christian Bible as well as the Qur'an, including Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses) and Yusuf (Joseph). Here, God saves Maryam (Mary) and her baby son `Isa (Jesus, a Prophet in Islam) from hunger, miraculously reviving a dead palm tree to provide them with dates to eat. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, Arabic text in gold naskh script, painting (on recto), from Stories of the Prophets (Qisas al-anbiya), by Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Nishapuri, possibly Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1570.

Per_232.c: Book of Testaments (Vaṣiyyatnāma). Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-dusted paper, with lacquered pasteboard covers, 10 folios, Persian script in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v), painting (fol. 5v, pasted in later, half of a double page composition), and pink borders with gold-painted designs of birds in scrollwork, floral trellis or animals on scrollwork throughout, lacquer covers with paired bird design, Book of Testaments (Vaṣiyyatnāma), instructions from the Prophet to Imām `Alī, colophon (fol. 10r) signed Shāh Maḥmūd Nishāpūrī, probably Tabriz, Iran, dated 923H, 1517.

Per_234.c: Anthology (Dīvān) of Persian poetry. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 53 folios, gilded leather binding, Persian verses in nasta`liq script, double page borders of two ducks and ten simurghs amid curling clouds (fols. 3v-4r) and illuminated cornerpieces (lachak) throughout, border designs of gold-outlined floral and foliate scrollwork or animals in landscape throughout, anthology (Dīvān) of different Persian poets including Sa`di, copied by Muhammad ibn `Ala' al-Din Raza'i, Iran, dated Jumada II 973H, January 1566. Folio 1r has a later owner's seal and signature, Sayyid `Ali Fu'ad, who owned the manuscript in 1278H (1861-62).

Per_235.t: Works of the Victorious (Āthār al-Muẓaffar) by Niẓām
Per_235.c: Works of the Victorious (Āthār al-Muẓaffar) by Niẓām. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 165 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated title heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v) and three paintings (fols. 55r, 132r, 152r), Works of the Victorious (Āthār al-Muẓaffar) by Niẓām, biography in verse of the Prophet Muḥammad, with emphasis on Shi`a lineage, originally composed in 1516 (922H) and dedicated to Khwāja Sayf al-Dīn Muẓaffar Beg, under Safavid shah Ismā`īl I (r. 1501-1524), unsigned, possibly Qazvin, Iran, dated 1 Rajab 974H, 12 January 1567.

Per_236.c: Garden (Būstān), by Sa`dī. Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-flecked paper, pressure-moulded leather binding with Persian poetry, 169 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated double frontispiece (chaharlawh, fols. 1v-2r), headings throughout, four paintings (fols. 50r, 57r, 59v, 143r) and later (c. 1900-1925, Europe) remargins, Garden (Būstān), by Sa`dī Shīrāzī (d. 1292), calligraphy attributed as if posthumously (fol. 169r), to Sulṭān `Alī Mashhadī (d. 1520), probably Tabriz, Iran, c. 1525, three of the paintings (fols. 50r, 57r, 143r) added Qazvin or Isfahan, c. 1590-1600.

Per_237.t: Attributes of Lovers (Ṣifāt al-'āshiqīn) by Hilālī (d. 1529)
Per_237.c: Attributes of Lovers (Ṣifāt al-'āshiqīn) by Hilālī (d. 1529). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, pressure-moulded and filigree leather bookbinding, 47 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh, fol. 2v), double page painting (fols. 1v-2r) and stencilled, gold-painted and cut-out (fol. 31 only) borders throughout, Attributes of Lovers (Ṣifāt al-'āshiqīn) by Badr al-Dīn of Astarābād, known as Hilālī Chaghatā'ī (d. 1529, Herat), unsigned, Iran, undated, c. 1590.

Per_238.t: Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār), by Jāmī (d. 1492)
Per_238.c: Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, pressure-moulded and filigree leather bookbinding, 71 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated double page (chahar-lawh, fols. 3v-4r), one painting (fol. 14v) and gold-painted borders of green, light blue, dark blue, cream, apricot or yellow paper (throughout), Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār, composed in 1481) by Nūr al-Dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), painting attributed here to Divāna Naqqāsh, unsigned, Bukhara, Uzbekistan, undated, c. 1560-1570. A further 4 folios detached from this codex volume are also in this museum collection: CBL Per 238.1, .2, .20, .46.

Per_238_1.t: Prince with his falconers, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492)
Per_238_1.c: Prince with his falconers, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492). A young prince on horseback is attended by servants, carrying his wine-flask and a parasol. Before him stand two falconers with their birds, one holding a freshly-caught rabbit. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, gold-painted floral designs with owner notes (on recto) and full-page painting (on verso), right half of double page frontispiece, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār) by Nūr al-Dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), detached from codex CBL Per 238, Bukhara, Uzbekistan, undated, c. 1560-1570.

Per_238_2.t: Horsemen hunting, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492)
Per_238_2.c: Horsemen hunting antelope, rabbits, wild ass, and a wolf, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, text-box left blank, with full-page painting (on recto), left half of double page frontispiece, and gold-painted lotus floral designs (on verso), from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār) by Nūr al-Dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), detached from codex CBL Per 238, Bukhara, Uzbekistan, undated, c. 1560-1570.

Per_238_20.t: Zulaykha pulls Yūsuf's coat as he leaves, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492)
Per_238_20.c: Zulaykha pulls Yūsuf's coat as he leaves, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492). Composed in 1481, Jāmī's poem contains 40 sections or "knots" (`aqd), each dedicated to a Sufi principle, with a narrative episode to illustrate the point. Here, the Qur'anic prophet Yūsuf (Joseph in the Old Testament) rushes away from his employer's wife Zulaykha (Potiphar's wife), resisting her attempts to seduce him. A golden statue sits in the alcove behind them, half-concealed by a curtain: Zulaykha had gone to draw the curtain over her sacred idol, so it could not watch them. Reflecting that his own God could see all things, Yūsuf left the room hastily. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with full page painting (on verso), from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār) by Nūr al-Dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), detached from codex CBL Per 238, Bukhara, Uzbekistan, undated, c. 1560-1570.

Per_238_46.t: The Sufi, the enslaved man, and the last camel, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492)
Per_238_46.c: The Sufi, the enslaved man, and the last camel, from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-abrār) by Jāmī (d. 1492). In this brief episode, a Sufi mystic meets with a merchant's encampment, and notices an enslaved African man chained in one of the tents. On asking the merchant to free him, the Sufi hears from the merchant why he now has only one camel left: earlier, the man’s beautiful singing so haunted the camel train, that once their packs were unloaded at the end of the day, the animals had run away. On requesting the man to sing once more, the Sufi was transfixed utterly by his song of longing, and the last camel broke its rope and escaped. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with full painting (on verso), from Rosary of the Pious (Subḥat al-Abrār) by Nūr al-Dīn `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (d. 1492), detached from codex CBL Per 238, text unsigned, painting attributed (lower margin) to Divāna Naqqāsh working from an older composition by Bihzād (“ṭarḥ Ustād Bih

Per_240_5.c: Chinese lion and kylin combat. In a writhing tangle of limbs, two creatures fight each other, with golden flames rippling from their bodies. They are supernatural beasts borrowed from Chinese mythology. Real animal fights were part of public entertainment in the grand square (maydan) of Safavid Isfahan, but there is a longer art history to this sort of image. Writing in the late 1590s, the chief court artist Sadiqi Beg Afshar (died 1610) praised animal combat designs as the best way to show an artist’s skill. He urged younger artists to aim for a powerful and original composition. Every limb must be engaged in the fight, in the ‘give and take’ (giroft-o-gir) of the struggle. Album folio, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, painting of Chinese-style mythical lion fighting a kylin, with illuminated corners, within ruled borders on gold-flecked dark blue frame, all mounted on dark blue card album page with gold-painted foliate scrollwork, blank blue card verso, painting unsigned,

Per_242_5.t: Groom leading his horse, by Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635)
Per_242_5.c: Groom leading his horse, by Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635). Album folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, tinted drawing of a man leading his horse down a rocky slope, signed “Reẓā drew it” (mashqahu Reẓā, on a rock beneath the horse), bordered with illumination panels and Persian text in nasta`liq script, extracts from the Rose Garden (Gulistān) by Sa`dī and the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi, within ruled borders on light blue-green paper frame with gold foliate scrollwork and further Persian verses, all mounted on green card album page with gold-painted floral scrollwork, drawing by Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), Isfahan, Iran, undated c. 1590-1600

Per_242_6.t: Seated dervish holding a flower, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635)
Per_242_6.c: Seated dervish holding a flower, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635). Album folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, tinted drawing of a smiling dervish seated holding a flower, with later Persian inscription (“raqam-e kamtarīn [...] fī shahr-e Jumada al-ukhra sanat 997H, below), within ruled borders on grey paper frame with gold foliation, on cream paper frame with inset Persian verses in nasta`liq script, on narrow cream paper frame with dark silver chevron lines, all mounted on cream card album folio with gold-painted plants and insects and oxidised silver patches, blank green fibrous verso, attributed here to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), probably Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1590-1600.

Per_246_1.t: Portrait of a man, by Shaykh `Abbāsī
Per_246_1.c: Portrait of a man, by Shaykh `Abbāsī. Admired and honoured by Shah `Abbas II, the artist Shaykh `Abbāsī created many strikingly refined portraits. This elegant image shows a young man in striped coat and turban, with sword and jewelled dagger at his waist, standing in a landscape. Shaykh `Abbāsī’s dated signature repeats his usual formula referring to the shah’s favour (“he acquired worth once he became Shaykh `Abbāsī”). Royal permission to use the name “`Abbāsī” must have added market value to the artist’s work, as well as prestige. Album folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, painting of a young man in striped coat and turban, with sword and jewelled dagger at his waist, standing in landscape, signed Shaykh `Abbāsī ("bahā gereft cho gardīd Shaykh `Abbāsī, 1076", reserved cartouche on right), within ruled borders on successive frames of gold-flecked peach, cream and dark blue paper, all mounted on plain grey card with leather strip along left edge, blank paper verso,

Per_246_2.t: Woman standing in landscape, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635)
Per_246_2.c: Woman standing in landscape, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635). Album folio, ink, colours and gold on gold-dusted cream paper, mounted on card, tinted drawing of a smiling woman standing in a landscape, holding a sash in one hand, with inscription panel in Persian above, within ruled borders on dark red paper frame with gold floral scrollwork, on gold-flecked pink paper frame, all mounted on cream card album page with gold-painted animals, birds and lotus scrollwork, blank fibrous green verso, drawing attributed here to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), Isfahan, Iran, c. 1600-1610.

Per_246_4.t: Seated young man offering fruit and wine
Per_246_4.c: Seated young man offering fruit and wine. Album folio, ink, colours and gold on blue paper, mounted on card, painting of seated young man in yellow coat and green turban, holding out a small fruit (apricot?) and a wine-cup, with gold painted landscape details on blue paper, within ruled borders on gold-flecked grey paper frame, then light blue paper frame with gold foliate scrollwork, all mounted on gold-flecked grey card album page, blank fibrous green verso, unsigned, Isfahan, Iran, c. 1600-1625.

Per_246_5.c: Woman kneeling alone. Wearing only purple trousers and a yellow sash, this woman kneels with her hands raised, as if in prayer. Her eyes gaze up towards the sun. Relatively rare, female nudity became more frequent in later Safavid painting, usually in reference to exotic foreigners. This drew from imported artworks of female allegories and fashionable portraiture, from Europe. Album folio, ink, colours and gold on blue paper, mounted on card, painting of kneeling woman in yellow scarf and purple trousers with gold bird detail, her palms raised in prayer, in a light green rocky landscape with the sun in upper left corner, framed with lines of Persian poetry in nasta`liq script, within ruled borders on gold-painted blue card album page, blank verso, unsigned, Isfahan, Iran, c. 1625-1650.

Per_247.t: Gift of the free (Tuḥfat al-aḥrār), by Jāmī (d. 1492)
a: `Abd al-Raḥmān Nūr al-Dīn Jāmī; Shah Husayn Shihabi al-Haravi
Per_247.c: Gift of the free (Tuḥfat al-aḥrār), by Jāmī (d. 1492). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather and pasteboard binding with gold, 77 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated double frontispiece (chahar-lawh, fols. 1v-2r), two paintings (fols. 34r, 69v), and gold-painted stencilled borders throughout, Gift of the Free (Tuḥfat al-aḥrār), by `Abd al-Raḥmān Nūr al-Dīn Jāmī (1414-1492), copied by Shāh Ḥusayn Shihābi al-Haravī, possibly Herat, Afghanistan, dated 993H, 1585

Per_251.c: Yūsuf and Zulaykhā, by Jāmī (d. 1492). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, green silk and leather covers, 177 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v) and five paintings (fols. 37r, 72r, 94r, 118r, 152v), Yūsuf and Zulaykhā, by `Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (1414-1492), colophon (fol. 177r) unsigned, probably Tabriz, Iran, dated 3 Jumada II 947H, 5 October 1540.

Per_254_65.t: `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib in single combat with `Amr ibn `Abd al-Wadd, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498)
Per_254_65.c: `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib in single combat with `Amr ibn `Abd al-Wadd, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from the Garden of purity on the lives of prophets, kings and caliphs (Rawḍat al-ṣafā fī sīrat al-anbiyā’ wa al-mulūk wa al-khulafā’), by Muḥammad Khawāndshāh ibn Maḥmūd, or Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498), volume 2 of his universal history, describes the biographies of the Prophet Muḥammad and the four Rashidun Caliphs, copied by Maḥmūd ibn Hājjī al-Jahramī, probably Shiraz, Iran, dated 24 Rajab 1003H, 4 April 1595.

Per_254_77.t: `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib wrenches the door from the fortress of Qamūṣ, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498)
Per_254_77.c: `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib wrenches the door from the fortress of Qamūṣ, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498). Mīr Khwānd describes the early conquests of the Muslims, including this victory over the Jewish fortress of Qamūṣ, which concluded the battle of Khaybar in 628. The Prophet Muḥammad watches from the right, as his son-in-law `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib pulls the door from the fortress, and uses it as a shield. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from the Garden of purity on the lives of prophets, kings and caliphs (Rawḍat al-ṣafā fī sīrat al-anbiyā’ wa al-mulūk wa al-khulafā’), by Muḥammad Khawāndshāh ibn Maḥmūd, or Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498), volume 2 of his universal history, describes the biographies of the Prophet Muḥammad and the four Rashidun Caliphs, copied by Maḥmūd ibn Hājjī al-Jahramī, probably Shiraz, Iran, dated 24 Rajab 1003H, 4 April 1595.

Per_254_128.t: Sasanian king Yazdagird III flees to the mill in Merv in 651, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498)
Per_254_128.c: Sasanian king Yazdagird III flees to the mill in Merv in 651, from the Garden of Purity (Rawḍat al-ṣafā) by Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498). Mīr Khwānd's history describes the early conquests by the Muslims, including their defeat of the Sasanian empire in Iran. Beaten on the battlefield in 642, the Sasanians' capital Ctesiphon (in modern Iraq) was sacked in 650. Final defeat came in 651, when the last Sasanian shah Yazdagird III fled, and took refuge by hiding in a water-mill, near the city of Merv (in modern Turkmenistan). Eventually the king was tracked down and killed, in 651. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto), from the Garden of purity on the lives of prophets, kings and caliphs (Rawḍat al-ṣafā fī sīrat al-anbiyā’ wa al-mulūk wa al-khulafā’), by Muḥammad Khawāndshāh ibn Maḥmūd, or Mīr Khwānd (d. 1498), volume 2 of his universal history, describes the biographies of the Prophet Muḥammad and the four Rashidun Caliphs, copied by Ma

Per_256_1.t: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_256_1.c: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Per_256_2.c: Farīdūn crosses the Tigris on his way to fight the tyrant Ẓaḥḥāk, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian verses in nasta`liq script, with framed rubric (recto: “Farīdūn goes to fight Ẓaḥḥāk, and crosses the river”) and painting (on verso), the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi, artist’s name (Miḥrāb?) inscribed above painting, probably Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1570-1585

Per_256_3.t: Tūr and Salm murder their brother Īraj, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_256_3.c: Tūr and Salm murder their brother Īraj, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian verses in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi, painting attributed Murād, probably Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1570-1585.

Per_256_4.t: The battle between Khusrau and Afrāsiyāb, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_256_4.c: The battle between Khusrau and Afrāsiyāb, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian verses in nasta`liq script, with framed rubric (recto: “battle between Afrāsiyāb and Khusrau”) and painting (on verso), the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi, painting attributed `Abdullāh Shīrāzī (Welch, 1976), probably Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1570-1585.

Per_256_5.t: Bīzhan is captured in Manīzha’s apartments, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_256_5.c: Bīzhan is captured in Manīzha’s apartments, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). The Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) describes the reigns of fifty ancient rulers of Iran, with dramatic sidestories about heroic champions of the court. In this episode, the young hero Bīzhan and the foreign princess Manīzha have fallen in love, even though their two countries have long been bitter enemies. She smuggles him into the palace, and they stay happily in her private apartments until her father the king finds out. Furious, the king sends the princess’s brother to arrest Bīzhan, and he is dragged away. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with two framed rubrics (recto) and painting (verso), from dispersed manuscript of the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi, artist’s name (Naqdī?) inscribed in right margin possibly Qazvin, Iran, c. 1570-1585.

Per_257.c: Anthology (Dīvān), by the poet Shāhī (d. 1453). The book of poetry opens to a double page scene, showing young men seated together in a garden. A prince, sitting against a cushion on a felt mat, listens to a friend reading out poems from a slim book (in the narrow "safina" format). On low tables there are long-necked wine bottles, of blue and white porcelain, or jewelled metal. Over the garden wall, flowering trees and a pollarded willow (with fresh green branches) show that it is springtime. Some of this manuscript's early ownership history is revealed through the addition of stamps and notes: these show that in June 1556, the book was in the imperial Mughal library in Delhi. At this date, emperor Akbar's father Humayun had died recently (in January 1556). His mother Hamida Banu Begum (1527-1604, Humayun's widow) may have been the book's next owner: her personal seal was added in 1560-61 (968H). Per_260_2.t: Youth in gold trousers, by Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635)
Per_260_2.c: Youth in gold trousers, by Rezā `Abbāsī (d. 1635). Dressed to the height of Safavid fashion, this young man is clasping a wine flask in both hands. A small cup tucks into the neckline of his shirt, and a dagger sits in the knot of his striped belt sash. His bird-patterned gold trousers, likely to be metal-brocaded silk, suggest a privileged life. Indeed the silk economy did bring prosperity to Safavid Isfahan, and many modern consumer habits as well. Reza has painted the man’s curling hair and the fur brim of his hat with remarkable lightness of touch. His signature on the lower left reads “work of the humble Reza `Abbasi”. Shah `Abbas granted Reza the honour of using the title “`Abbasi”, to show his status in the royal court. Folio, ink, colours and gold on gold-dusted paper, mounted on card, painting of a young man wearing a fur-brimmed felt hat, purple jacket with gold clouds, blue striped sash (with tucked dagger) and gold trousers with bird design, and clasping a bottle with a win

Per_260_3.t: Kneeling man offering wine, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635)
Per_260_3.c: Kneeling man offering wine, possibly by Reza `Abbasi (d. 1635) A young man holds out a small footed glass of red wine, to an unseen companion. The wine vessels and fruit suggest that a garden party is in progress, with willow and poplar trees painted in gold. The man’s dark red coat has a lavish gold design of songbirds. Reza’s signature floats just above the wine cup, offering the artwork as “work of the most humble Reza `Abbasi”. Album folio, ink, colours and gold on grey paper, mounted on card, painting of a kneeling youth in dark red coat with gold bird details, green sash and fur-brimmed yellow hat, holding out a footed glass of red wine, with ceramic and metal vessels and fruit on the lower left, inscribed "work of the humble Reẓā `Abbāsī " (raqam-e kamīneh Reẓā `Abbāsī, left), within ruled borders on dark brown paper frame with gold streaks, mounted on pink card with gold-painted foliate trellis, blank grey card verso, Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1630-1635.

Per_260_8.t: Old man with a small child, by Ṣādiqī (d. 1610)
Per_260_8.c: Old man with a small child, by Ṣādiqī (d. 1610). Possibly drawn from a European print source, this tinted drawing shows an old man leaning on a staff, and leading a child by the hand. The artist was Shah `Abbas’s head librarian (kitabdar), the director of the royal court atelier. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, mounted on card, (on recto:) tinted drawing of an old man leaning on a staff, leading a child by the hand, signed Ṣādiqī (rāqamhu Ṣādiqī) in archaic script, with a verse of Persian poetry in nasta`liq script above and below, mounted together in gold-flecked blue paper frame, (on verso:) four lines of Persian poetry in nasta`liq script, signed Mīr `Alī al-Kātib, with illuminated cornerpieces, mounted in blue paper frame with gold foliate scrollwork, album page of plain card, possibly Isfahan, Iran, c. 1590-1610.

Per_262.c: Anthology (Dīvān), by Fāryābi (d. 1201). This manuscript was made for the library of Husayn Khan Shamlu, who ruled as the governor of Safavid Herat from 1598 to 1618. His name is written across the tent doorway in one lively scene (fol. 80r) of musicians and revellers enjoying a party in the countryside. Throughout Iran, many centres of power lay in the provinces far beyond the capital, controlled by regional governors appointed by the shah. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 91 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated title page (sarlawh, fol. 1v), colophon (fol. 91r) and headings throughout, 3 paintings (fols. 32v, 67v, 80r), and replaced outer borders (fols. 1-33, 66-91), Anthology (Dīvān), by Ẓahīr al-Dīn Abū al-Faẓl Ṭāhir Fāryābī (1156-1201, Tabriz), produced for the library (kitābkhāna) of Ḥusayn Khān Shāmlū (Safavid governor of Herat, 1598-1618), copied by Shāh Qāsim, Herat, Afghanistan, dated Jumada I 1023H, June 1614.

Per_263.t: Folios from a Book of Constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita)
Per_263.c: Folios from a Book of Constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita). These loosely bound folios may have been intended for a copy of al-Sufi's well-known Book of the Constellations: each page features a single painting of a classical constellation figure, such as Cassiopeia or Pegasus. The same figure is then repeated on the reverse side of each folio, shown in mirror image. This shows the constellation first as it appears in the sky, and then as it appears on a celestial globe. The stars are painted as gold circles, but there are no captions, labels or text. Later copies of this work are often organised in this way, showing that the painter and the scribe worked separately. Normally, these illustrated folios would next be added into a manuscript, and inserted into the correct chapters to complete the treatise. Codex, 22 folios, colours and gold on paper, 22 constellation figures, no text or labels, probably produced for insertion into a copy of the Book of Constellations (Kitāb ṣ

Per_265_1.t: Portrait of a woman, by Mu`īn Muṣavvir
Per_265_1.c: Portrait of a woman, by Mu`in Musavvir. Folio, ink and colours on paper, mounted on card, (on recto:) tinted drawing of a smiling woman with long sleeves crossed at the wrists and holding a feathered ornament, clouds and bird overhead, signed by Mu`in Musavvir, mounted in dark cream paper frame, (on verso:) blank, on very thin paper album page, Isfahan, Iran, dated (inscription in red, on left:) Tuesday 3 Dhu'l-Hijja 1051H, 5 March 1642.

Per_265_2.t: Boy with Cockerel, by Mu`īn Muṣavvir
Per_265_2.c: Boy with Cockerel, by Mu`īn Muṣavvir. A boy stoops slightly as if he is about to release the large cockerel to the ground — this may be a fighting cock about to do battle. The artist has written a note on the lower left, dedicating his drawing to his son Aqa Zaman, “drawn in haste”. He often signed (and dated) his work in this way, writing directly onto the drawing, and drawing attention to the immediate moment of making the image. Folio, ink and colours on paper, mounted on grey card, (on recto:) tinted drawing of a boy carrying a large cockerel (possibly a fighting cock), signed by Mu`īn Muṣavvir, mounted in light pink paper frame, (on verso:) blank, on grey album page, Isfahan, Iran, dated 15 Dhu’l-Hijja 1066H, 4 October 1656.

Per_265_4.t: Seated man in his coat, by Muḥsin
Per_265_4.c: Seated man in his coat, by Muḥsin. Wrapped in his fur-trimmed coat, a man crouches against the cold. His shaved head and large moustache make a strong contrast with the younger men in typical Safavid portraits. Nonetheless this was court fashion too. In 1618, the Italian traveller Pietro della Vale (died 1652) met Shah `Abbas I and travelled with him on military campaign in northern Iran: he later described the king’s shaven head and distinctive drooping moustache. Folio, ink, colours and gold on greenish paper, mounted on black-stencilled cream card, (recto:) tinted drawing of a seated man wrapped in his fur-trimmed coat, signed Muḥsin (lower left), with gold-flecked paper panels mounted above and below, mounted together in ruled frame, on album page, (verso:) backed with blank paper, Isfahan, Iran, dated 1025H, 1615.

Per_265_5.c: Portrait of a Safavid official. This finely-observed portrait shows a well-dressed, bearded man with blue eyes and a piercing gaze. The set of his shoulders may show a spinal disability. His striped turban and fur-lapelled blue coat suggest wealth, and his slight frown suggests power. Album folio, colours and gold on paper, mounted on pink card, painting of a man in striped turban and gold brocaded blue coat with fur lapels, holding a rod, unsigned, within ruled borders on bright pink paper frame, then purple paper frame, all mounted on pink card album page, blank paper verso, Isfahan, Iran, c. 1650-1700.

Per_268.t: Burning and Melting (Sūz u Gawdāz) by Naw`ī Khabushānī
Per_268.c: Burning and Melting (Suz u Gawdaz) by Nau`i Khabushani. Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-sprinkled paper, leather binding with gold, 34 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with 10 paintings, Burning and Melting (Sūz u Gawdāz) by Muḥammad Reẓā Khabushānī known as Naw`ī (d. 1610, Burhanpur), poem composed in India for Mughal prince Daniyal (1581-1614), son of Akbar, paintings attributed to Muḥammad Qāsim, Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1650-1660.

Per_269.t: Burning and Melting (Sūz u Gawdāz) by Naw`ī Khabushānī (d. 1610)
Per_269.c: Burning and Melting (Sūz u Gawdāz) by Naw`ī Khabushānī (d. 1610). Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-sprinkled paper, later binding with lacquer vignettes in each doublure, 29 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sawlawh, fol. 1v), gold-painted foliate borders (fols. 1v-2r) and 12 paintings, Burning and Melting (Sūz u Gawdāz) by Muḥammad Reẓā Khabushānī known as Naw`ī (d. 1610, Burhanpur), poem composed in India for Mughal prince Daniyal (1581-1614), son of Akbar, paintings unsigned, text copied by `Abd al-Rashīd, Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1650-1660, later binding c. 1800-1825.

Per_270.t: Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi (d. 1020), illustrated by Mu`īn Muṣavvir
Per_270.c: Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Abū al-Qāsim Firdausi (d. 1020), illustrated by Mu`īn Muṣavvir. This is the second volume of a two-volume Shahnama. The first volume, now in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto, is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its thirty-three paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Volume two (CB Per 270) has no full date recorded at the end of the text, but the last of its twenty-two paintings (on fol. 223r) is dated Muhammad 1066H (November 1655). These dates allow a reconstruction of how the set was produced: the text was copied first, and the fifty-five paintings followed - over a three year period. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, modern gilded red leather binding, 223 folios (a further 12 folios are detached and mounted separately), Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated double page frontispiece (fols. 1v-2r), framed rubrics throughout and 12 paintings (fols. 31v, 44r, 48r, 83v, 89v, 95r, 110v, 175r, 186v, 197v, 216r, 223r), folios

Per_270_16.t: Gushtasp wrongly sends his son Isfandiyar to prison, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_16.c: Gushtasp wrongly sends his son Isfandiyar to prison, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Sitting in the palace surrounded by his protesting courtiers, King Gushtasp falsely accuses his son Isfandiyar of treason, and sentences him to imprisonment in a mountain fortress. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting and framed rubric ("Gushtasp approaches Rustam", both on verso), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_25.t: Isfandiyar kills the dragon, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_25.c: Isfandiyar kills the dragon, from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) by Firdausi. Isfandiyar rides inside his spiked chariot towards the giant dragon, painted in the folio margin as it climbs down the mountainside towards him. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with framed rubric ("The Third Trial: Isfandiyar kills the dragon", in white) and painting (both on verso), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_26.t: Isfandiyar defeats the sorceress, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_26.c: Isfandiyar defeats the sorceress, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. For his fourth heroic trial, prince Isfandiyar captures a sorceress with an iron lasso, breaking her spell to reveal her true form, and then killing her with his sword. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on verso), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_53.t: Rustam shoots Shaghad from the spiked pit, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_53.c: Rustam shoots Shaghad from the spiked pit, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Fatally trapped with his champion horse Rakhsh in a pit of poisoned spikes, Rustam shoots an arrow at his betrayer Shaghad, piercing a tree trunk to kill him. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with rubric ("Rustam pins Shaqad to a tree with an arrow", in white) and painting (on recto), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_66.t: Iskandar marries Roshanak, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī
Per_270_66.c: Iskandar marries Roshanak, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. The poet Firdausi describes Iskandar’s conquests, including his defeat of the Iranian king Dara. This reflects Alexander’s victory over Darius III (died 330 BC), when the invader burned the Achaemenid palace of Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid). Here Iskandar marries the Persian princess Roshanak at Istakhr, which is the name Firdausi uses for Persepolis. There is a small grey face in their palace wall: this may refer to the stone reliefs that were then visible at the ruins of Persepolis. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270, dated 1066H (1655) on fol. 223r), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Per_270_80.t: Iskandar in the Land of Darkness, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausi
Per_270_80.c: Iskandar in the Land of Gloom, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. One of the kings in Firdausi’s epic Book of Kings is Iskandar, or the historic Alexander III of Macedon (died 323 BC). He is known in European tradition as Alexander the Great. Firdausi tells the stories of Iskandar’s many military conquests, but this scene shows a more spiritual adventure. Iskandar rides with his companions to the west, looking for the Water of Life that will make him immortal. His group includes a man in a tall white turban that is Ottoman in fashion: the Isfahan-based painter has placed him as a marker for all regions west of Safavid Iran. Iskandar’s guide through the Land of Darkness is Khidr, who is a saintly figure in Islam. Travelling through the dark, Iskandar and his entourage lose sight of Khidr, and so the world conqueror misses the miraculous water source. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270, dated 1066H (1655) on fol.

Per_270_106.t: Shapur is enthroned as an infant, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_106.c: Shapur is enthroned as an infant, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Born shortly after his father Narsi's death, Shapur is enthroned as a baby, and attended by servants and courtiers. His mother rests in the upstairs pavilion, on the upper left. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_109.t: The Romans appoint Baranush as their new Caesar, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_109.c: The Romans appoint Baranush as their new Caesar, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Following total defeat by Shapur of Iran, the Romans appoint the wise Baranush as their new Caesar. He reflects on the war, and writes a letter of peace to Shapur. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with framed rubric ("Caesar's brother Yanus fights Shapur and is defeated", in white) and painting (on verso), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi (codex CB Per 270), painting signed Mu'in Musavvir, Isfahan, Iran, 1655.

Per_270_163.t: Bahram Chubina returns thoughtfully to his companions, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_163.c: Bahram Chubina returns thoughtfully to his companions, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Having heard an encouraging prediction at a magical fortress in the wilderness, Bahram Chubina rejoined his hunting companions without explaining, and began to dream of future power, glory and rebellion against king Hormozd. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and two framed rubrics ("Bahram becomes rebellious to Hormozd, and Khirad-Burzin abandons him" in white, "The priest interprets events, and Hormozd sends Bahram the basket of broken daggers as a warning"

Per_270_189.t: Battle between Khusrau Parviz and the rebellious Bahram Chubina, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_270_189.c: Battle between Khusrau Parviz and the rebellious Bahram Chubina, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Evenly matched, the forces of Khusrau Parviz and Bahram Chubina battle intensely, with both leaders fighting each other. The following night, Khusrau's herald calls out an amnesty for all of Bahram's soldiers, and they abandon his camp before dawn comes. This is one of ten folios detached from its codex (also in the Chester Beatty collection, Per 270), the second volume in a two-volume set of this text, illustrated by the Isfahan painter Mu`in Musavvir. Volume one is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (Ms22): its colophon is dated Jumada II 1064H (April 1654), with four of its paintings dated 1065H or 1067H (1654-1657). Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and two framed rubrics ("Bahram flees Hormozd" in white, "Bahram arrives to the old woman, her words, and his weariness" in red, on verso), from the Book of Kings

Per_273.t: De Materia Medica (Kitāb al-Ḥashā’ish fī hayūlā al-ṭibb) by Dioscorides (d. c. 90) in Persian translation by Ghiyāth al-Dīn Muḥammad Reẓavī
Per_273.c: De Materia Medica (Kitāb al-Ḥashā’ish fī hayūlā al-ṭibb) by Dioscorides (d. c. 90) in Persian translation by Ghiyāth al-Dīn Muḥammad Reẓavī. Codex, ink and colours on paper, 203 folios, black leather bookbinding with gold-painted floral corner details and central lobed medallion and pendants of birds and butterflies among roses (gol-o-bolbol) painted in lacquer technique, red leather doublures with gold-painted outline decoration, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with paintings of plants, animals and occasionally people throughout, De Materia Medica (Kitāb al-Ḥashā’ish fī hayūlā al-ṭibb) by Dioscorides (d. c. 90), on the medicinal uses of plants, animals and minerals, books 1-4 only, Persian translation from an earlier Arabic translation from the original Greek pharmacopia, this translation by Ghiyāth al-Dīn Muḥammad Reẓavī ordered by Safavid shah `Abbās I (r. 1588-1629), text unsigned, one painting (fol. 50r) signed Darvīsh Salīm, another (fol. 145r) signed Malek Ḥusayn and dated 105

Per_274_2.t: Opening folio from the Garden (Būstān), by Sa`dī
Per_274_2.c: Opening folio from the Garden (Būstān), by Sa`dī. Per_276_205.t: Bahram Gur and the Iranian princess in the white pavilion, from Seven Portraits (Haft Paykar), in the Five Poems (Khamsa), by Nizami
a: Muḥammad Muqim, attributed to; Mulla Barqi
Per_276_205.c: Bahram Gur and the Iranian princess in the white pavilion, from Seven Portraits (Haft Paykar), in the anthology of Five Poems (Khamsa), by Nizami. Nizami's Seven Portraits tells how prince Bahram marries seven princesses from the seven world regions, and orders a pavilion built for each bride within his palace. Following cosmic order, each world region has a specific colour, virtue, ruling planet and day of the week, and Bahram's seven pavilions are themed accordingly. Each night, he visits one princess, who tells him a story. The week ends in the white pavilion on Friday, when Bahram visits the Iranian princess, attended by her servants and musicians, and listens to her story. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (unsigned, attributed to Muhammad Muqim, on recto), from Seven Portraits (Haft Paykar), in the anthology Five Poems (Khamsa), by Nizami (1141-1209), copied by Mulla Barqi and Mulla `Arabshah, ordered by librarian (kitabdar) `A

Per_277.t: Partial copy of the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Abū al-Qāsim Firdausī (d. 1020)
Per_277.c: Partial copy of the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Abū al-Qāsim Firdausī (d. 1020). Together with twelve detached folios also in the Chester Beatty collection, this codex forms only part of the original manuscript, produced at the Safavid court in Iran, in the late sixteenth century. The rest of the codex is now lost, including the final folio which would usually include a colophon statement about the patron, calligrapher's name, place of production and date. Nonetheless, the illuminator has signed the elaborate title panel on fol.1v: at the centre of the green border frame is written the name Zayn al-`Abidin al-Tabrizi. This artist was noted in Qadi Ahmad's 1596-1606 record of court calligrapher and painters, as a specialist in gilding, painting and portraiture, who worked in the shah's workshop (kar-khana) all his life. Per_277_3.t: The sīmurgh arrives to assist Rūdāba with the birth of Rustam, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
a: Muhammad Zaman ibn Haji Yusuf; Unknown
Per_277_3.c: The simurgh arrives to assist Rūdāba with the birth of Rustam, by Muḥammad Zamān. The simurgh (a giant magical bird) flies down into the picture-frame, in response to an appeal from her former foster-son Zal, during the labour of his wife Rūdāba. With the noble simurgh's help, Rūdāba gives birth (via Caesarean section) to Rustam, who will grow up to become the great hero of Firdausi's epic. A specialist painter in the European mode (farangi-saz, in Persian), Isfahan court painter Muḥammad Zamān was appointed to add modern paintings to this older manuscript from the royal library, in 1675-6. Per_277_5.t: Faridun’s sons meet King Sarv of Yemen and his daughters, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_277_5.c: Faridun’s sons meet King Sarv of Yemen and his daughters, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. King Sarv of Yemen sits in the centre, with his three daughters on the left, and the three sons of Faridun on the right, in a palace courtyard with garden landscape beyond. Sarv begrudgingly accepts that his daughters may now marry the Iranian princes, because the boys have solved his riddle. On the upper right, a woman (the girls' mother) sits alone on a balcony, and there is an empty nest in the plane tree overhead. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and illuminated rubric ("Faridun tests his sons", both on verso), with gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Abu al-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1020), attributed to the early reign of Safavid Shah `Abbas I (r. 1587-1629), Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1590-1600. Per_277_7.t: Salm and Tūr send an envoy to the court of their father Farīdūn, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_277_7.c: Salm and Tūr send an envoy to the court of their father Farīdūn, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī (d. 1020). This court scene continues the story of Farīdūn, in Firdausī’s Book of Kings. Now ruling Iran as a just and noble king, Farīdūn decides to split his kingdom among his three sons. This turns out to be a mistake that will end in tragedy. His two older sons are disgusted when each is appointed to rule a distant region, while Farīdūn's youngest son receives the central lands of Iran. Here, the two brothers send a messenger to their father’s court, to complain. Anxiety fills the faces of both king and messenger, while the others seem blissfully unaware of the conflict that will surely follow. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated panels and rubric ("Salm and Tūr send an envoy", all on recto) and painting (on verso), with gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Abū al-Qāsim Firdausī (d. 1020), attribut

Per_277_9.t: The White Dīv captures and blinds Kay Kāvus, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_277_9.c: The White Dīv captures and blinds Kay Kāvus, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Against all advice, king Kay Kāvus decided to invade Mazandaran, where he and his army were magically blinded by the spells of the White Div (or demon), and are now being kept captive. They will have to be rescued by the hero Rustam. Comically unrefined, the White Div nonetheless has a resigned air as he addresses his foolish prisoner. This folio belongs to a later campaign of artwork, led by the Isfahan artist Muḥammad Zamān, to add dramatic new illustrations to an older manuscript in the Safavid royal library. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated panels (on recto), painting (on verso) and gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Abū al-Qāsim Firdausī (d. 1020), manuscript attributed to the early reign of Safavid Shah `Abbās I (r. 1587-1629), Qazvin or Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1590-1600, this painting (and possibly

Per_277_11.t: Rudaba lets down her hair for Zal, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_277_11.c: Rudaba lets down her hair for Zal, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Rudaba is the daughter of Mehrab, king of Kabul, and she has fallen in love with Zal, son of the ruler of Zabulestan in Iran. The couple overcome family and cultural objections by meeting in secret. Rudaba offers her long hair for Zal to climb to her room, but instead he lassoes the palace battlements, and climbs up by rope. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with gold-painted borders, and painting (on recto), from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Abu al-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1022), attributed to the early reign of Safavid Shah `Abbas I (r. 1587-1629), Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1590-1600. This is one of twenty-two folios in the Chester Beatty, all from the same partial copy (possibly never fully completed) of Firdausi's Shahnama: ten folios are in a modern binding, twelve are mounted separately. Per_277_12.t: The simurgh carries Zal to her nest, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_277_12.c: The simurgh carries Zal to her nest, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. When Zal is born with white hair, his father Sam presumes this a bad omen, and the nobleman has the baby abandoned in the wilderness. There, the simurgh (a giant magical bird) finds him, and carries him back to her three simurgh chicks, seen in this painting, as they wait expectantly in their mountaintop nest. The dramatic moment is painted in vivid colour, with the steep rocky precipice jutting up out of the picture-frame, and the exquisitely-painted simurgh spreading her wings. When the simurgh reaches the nest with Zal, the chicks refuse to eat him, and so Zal is adopted into the family. Later in the story, the white-haired boy is reunited with his remorseful father, and Zal grows up to become a pivotal character in the Shahnama. Per_277_13.c: Rustam kills Zal’s white elephant, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. While still a boy, Rustam uses his heroic strength to kill a mad elephant, with his grandfather's mace. Impressed, his father Zal decides to send Rustam on his first mission, to avenge his great-grandfather's death at the fortress of Sipand. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto), illuminated rubric ("Zal sends Rustam to seize the fortress of Sipand", on verso) and gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Abu al-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1022), attributed to the early reign of Safavid Shah `Abbas I (r. 1587-1629), Qazvin, Iran, undated, c. 1590-1600. Per_277_14.c: Farīdūn crosses the Tigris on his way to fight Ẓaḥḥāk, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī. Per_277_15.t: Manuchihr pursuing Tūr, his father's murderer, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī
Per_277_15.c: Manūchihr pursuing Tūr, his father's murderer, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī. To complete Firdausi’s tale of king Farīdūn, the injustice of Iraj’s murder is finally resolved a generation later. Iraj’s grown son Manūchihr rides after one of the murderers, his uncle Tūr, and will shortly avenge his innocent father’s death. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (on recto) and gold-painted borders, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma) by Firdausī (d. 1020), folio produced Qazvin or Isfahan, Iran, c. 1590-1600, this painting (or possibly entire folio) added as part of an intervention led by Muḥammad Zamān, Isfahan, Iran, 1675-1676.
