Per_277_16.t: Salm and Tūr organise the murder of their brother Īraj, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
a: Muhammad Zaman ibn Haji Yusuf; Unknown
Per_277_16.c: Salm and Tūr organise the murder of their brother Īraj, by Muḥammad Zamān, from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Angry over the succession plan, the two embittered sons of Farīdūn have organised the murder of their innocent brother Īraj. They send his head to their horrified father, seated here on the left. Farīdūn is dressed in contemporary Safavid fashion, and he may be understood also as Muḥammad Zamān's royal patron, Shah Sulaymān. The scene takes place in front of a European architectural composition in startling illusionistic perspective. The source image was a print by the Dutch artistprintmaker Hendrik Hondius (died 1650), adapted in turn from Hans Vredeman de Vries (died 1607). A specialist painter in the European mode (farangi-saz, in Persian), Isfahan court painter Muḥammad Zamān was appointed to add modern paintings to this older manuscript from the royal library, in 1675-6. Per_277_17.t: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma)
Per_277_17.c: Ṭahmūras defeats the demon army, attributed to Reẓā `Abbāsī (d. 1635), from the Book of Kings (Shāhnāma). Across a rocky mountain, king Ṭahmūras and his army defeat the rebellious dīvs (or demons). On horseback, Ṭahmūras delivers a blow with his mace to the Black Dīv, while his forces scatter the others. The demons offer to surrender, and promise in return for peace that they will teach the art of reading and writing to mankind. Tahmuras learns almost thirty scripts. Per_277_22.t: Rustam's horse Rakhsh fights a lion while Rustam sleeps, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_277_22.c: Rustam's horse Rakhsh fights a lion while Rustam sleeps, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. Pausing during a long journey, the hero Rustam sleeps while his brave horse Rakhsh fights and kills a lion. On waking up, Rustam scolds the horse for risking his own life as well as their mission to Mazandaran, to save the king of Iran from the White Div. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, pasted to card, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with painting (unfinished) and gold-painted borders (on recto), and blank verso, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Abu al-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1022), folio possibly produced Qazvin, Iran, c. 1590-1600, this painting worked as part of an intervention led by Muhammad Zaman, Isfahan, Iran, 1675-1676. Per_278.t: History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl)
Per_278.c: History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl). The dramatic military successes of Ismā`īl I (r. 1501-1524) were remembered for generations, in works of formal history as well as in popular story-telling tradition. One of a number of similar anonymous histories, this manuscript was made in 1683 in Isfahan, under the second-last of the Safavid shahs, Sulaymān (reigned 1666–1694). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 245 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with title heading (sarlawh, fol. 1v), 18 paintings (fols. 20r, 47v, 77r, 89v, 119v, 136v, 149r, 152v, 160r, 162v, 167v, 176v, 191r, 193r, 195r, 197v, 199v, 215r), History of the world-adorning Shāh Ismā`īl (Tārīkh-e jahānārā-ye Shāh Ismā`īl bahādur khān), anonymous, account of the Safavid dynasty from Ismā`īl I (r. 1501-1524) to `Abbās II (r. 1642-1666) copied by Muḥtashim Iṣfahānī (colophon fol. 245v), Isfahan, Iran, dated Monday 16 Safar1094H, 14 February 1683.

Per_279.t: History of the Safavid shahs up to 1667, by Murtaẓā Qulī
Per_279.c: History of the Safavid shahs up to 1667, by Murtaẓā Qulī. Codex, ink, colours and gold on gold-sprinkled paper, lacquer book covers, 138 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated title page (sarlawh, fol. 1v) and gold foliate borders (fols. 1v-2r), and 22 paintings, (1: fols. 1v-86) untitled history of the Safavid shahs up to the initial accession of Safī II in 1666 (1077H), composed 1667-1668 (1087H) by Murtaẓā Qulī, Ardabil shrine guardian, (2: fols. 87-138r) poetry, (3: fols. 1r, 138v) verses signed `Alī Reẓā al-Kātib, paintings signed Muẓaffar `Alī (fols. 6v, 44r, 63v) and Reẓā-ye Muṣavvir (fol. 11r, 17v, 27v, 32v), Isfahan, Iran, undated, c. 1670.

Per_292_2.t: Angels above the Ka`ba in Mecca, folio from a dispersed anthology
Per_292_2.c: Angels above the Ka`ba in Mecca, folio from a dispersed anthology. This night-scene shows rows of angels among golden clouds, two of whom carry a covered tray, billowing scented smoke to represent blessings (barakat). Far below them is the Ka`ba sanctuary in Mecca, with pilgrims around it. The angels all face toward the right, because this painting is from a double-page composition: on the opposite page (Chester Beatty Per 292.1), the Prophet Muhammad rides his magical steed Buraq through the skies, accompanied by more angels, on his Night Journey (Mir`raj) or Ascension (Isra'). This image was often used for the opening pages of poetry anthologies, together with verses praising the Prophet. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian poetry in nasta`liq script with full-page painting (recto), left side of a double-page composition, folio trimmed and remounted on album page, Shiraz, Iran, c. 1410.

Per_292_3.t: Rustam kills the dragon, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi
Per_292_3.c: Rustam kills the dragon, from the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. The hero Rustam undertakes seven heroic trials (haft khan), while travelling to Mazandaran to rescue his king, Kay Kavus. Here, for his third feat, he charges his brave horse Rakhsh into a fire-breathing dragon, and kills it. Folio, colours and gold on paper, single framed painting, probably cut down from a manuscript folio for re-mounting in an album (muraqqa`), Iran, c. 1450.

Per_293_1.c: Sa`d fights the demon army, from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470). In a rocky landscape, the hero Sa`d-e Vaqqāṣ charges his horse towards one demon (or dīv), striking it with his mace, while his valiant horse tramples another two. Meanwhile four more demons hurl down rocks from all sides. In the silver sea, beneath a scaly sea-monster in the lower left corner, the painter Farhād has signed his name and written the date 881H (1476-77). Composed in 1426-1427 (830H), Ibn Ḥusām’s epic Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) tells the mythologised adventures of five heroes of Shi`a Islam: Imām `Alī (`Ali ibn Abī Ṭālib, d. 661, son-in-law of the Prophet Muḥammad) and his four companions Sa`d-e Vaqqāṣ (Sa`d ibn Abī Waqqāṣ), Abū al-Meḥjan (`Abdullāh Abū Miḥjan), Mālik-e Azhdar (Mālik al-Ashtar), and the heroic trickster (`ayyār) `Amr-e Omayya (`Amr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī). Per_293_2.c: Mir Sayyāf cuts off the king's arm in the palace garden, from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470). Per_293_3.c: Mālik-e Azhdar rides out from the palace with his soldiers, folio from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470). Per_293_5.c: The King of the East listens to a messenger, folio from the Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) by Ibn Ḥusām (d. 1470). Composed in 1426-1427 (830H), Ibn Ḥusām’s epic Book of the East (Khāvarānnāma) tells the mythologised adventures of five heroes of Shi`a Islam: Imām `Alī (`Ali ibn Abī Ṭālib, d. 661, son-in-law of the Prophet Muḥammad) and his four companions Sa`d-e Vaqqāṣ (Sa`d ibn Abī Waqqāṣ), Abū al-Meḥjan (`Abdullāh Abū Miḥjan), Mālik-e Azhdar (Mālik al-Ashtar), and the heroic trickster (`ayyār) `Amr-e Omayya (`Amr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī). Through their collective strength and resourcefullness, the righteous five gradually conquer all the pagan kings and fortresses of "the lands of the East" for Islam. Along the way they also defeat supernatural monsters and overcome magical challenges and talismans. Per_294.c: Timurid Anthology of Six Persian Poets. This manuscript was made in Timurid Shiraz, in the 1430s. Although now in damaged and incomplete condition, this was a magnificent court production, shown by the complex illuminated medallions, the paintings and the paper itself. Five of the pages were made not in Iran but in Ming China: these heavily-sized olive green folios are block-printed with meandering gold designs. There are other known examples of the same heavy Chinese paper used in Timurid manuscripts, and Iranian papermakers soon imitated the fashion for gold-decorated coloured pages. The Timurid courts exchanged several embassies with Ming China at this period, including one 1419-22 mission with the artist Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash in the delegation. Per_295.c: Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi. This large copy of Firdausi's epic poem has fifty-nine paintings, depicting the adventures of Iran's ancient kings, queens, heroes, villains and monsters. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 547 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, illuminated headings and shamsa medallion (its text deliberately erased), 59 paintings (some faces retouched, or flaking to reveal the underdrawing), the Book of Kings (Shahnama) by Firdausi, text copied by Muhammad Ma`sum ibn Sultan Muhammad al-Haravi, possibly Khurasan, Iran, dated 8 Dhu'l-Hijjah 950H, 3 February 1544, paintings possibly dateable (by style) c. 1575

Per_297_6.t: Ascension of the Prophet (Mi`raj), from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di
a: Muhammad Sharif, attributed to; Mir Salih al-Katib
Per_297_6.c: Ascension of the Prophet (Mi`raj), from the Garden (Bustān) of Sa`di. The Ascension and Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad is noted in the Qur'an, and many later writers have described and praised this mystical narrative, including the poet Sa`di. Surrounded by golden flames (to show holiness), the Prophet rides through the night sky, upon his magical steed Buraq, with a retinue of angels. His guide is the angel Jibril (Gabriel, on the upper left), who leads the Prophet on his journey to the furthest mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa'), to the circles of hell and heaven, and then back. Folio, ink, colours and gold on paper, Persian text in nasta`liq script, full-page painting (on recto, attributed Muhammad Sharif), from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di, copied by Mir Salih al-Katib, possibly Bukhara, Uzbekistan, c. 1570, this painting one of eleven later added, for the library (kitabkhana) of Hidayat ibn Mir Mu`in al-Din Khwaja `Abd al-Rahim Juybari (d. 1628), possibly at the dynastic Sufi shr

Per_297_22.t: Jamshīd writes on the rockface, from the Garden (Būstān) by Sa`dī (d. 1291)
a: Muḥammad Sharīf, attributed to; Mīr Sāliḥ al-Kātib
Per_297_22.c: The king's graffiti, from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di. The poet Sa`di tells this brief tale about Jamshīd, the mythical wise king from ancient Iran: the verses are written around the frame of this painting. While riding in the wilderness, the king stopped beside a flowing mountain stream. Inspired by its everlasting beauty, he wrote some lines of poetry onto the nearby rockface: “At this spring, just as I do today, many other kings have lived and breathed before my time, and they have passed on since then. We all seized the world by force, but not one of us could take it with us to the grave”. In this painting, the king's servants stand waiting, one of them holding his pencase and inkpot. In black ink on the rock, the king has already written the first words of his message “at this spring…” The king’s graffiti leaves a reflective message for future readers, who may also stop at this beautiful place and think about the temporary nature of power. Per_297_184.t: Preparing the palace feast, from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di
a: Muhammad Murad Samarqandi, attributed to; Mir Salih al-Katib
Per_297_184.c: Preparing the palace feast, from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di. This busy scene shows palace cooks working to prepare and serve up a feast. A fire blazes under a cauldron, while the cook skins a carcass for a meat stew, and a row of covered dishes waits on the grass. On the lower left, a dervish and child beg for food. On the right, servants line up to enter the palace: this painting is the left half of a double page scene, and the opposite page (fol. 183v, in the codex, Per 297) shows the prince and his guests inside the palace. Folio, colours and gold on paper, painting (on recto, attributed Muhammad Murad Samarqandi, left side of a double-page composition), from the Garden (Bustān), by Sa`di, copied by Mir Salih al-Katib, possibly Bukhara, Uzbekistan, c. 1570, this painting one of eleven later added, for the library (kitabkhana) of Hidayat ibn Mir Mu`in al-Din Khwaja `Abd al-Rahim Juybari (d. 1628), possibly at the dynastic Sufi shrine complex of Char Bakr, Sumitan, near Bukhara, Uz

Per_298_7.t: Portrait of Safavid Shah Sulaymān (d. 1694), by Shaykh `Abbāsī
Per_298_7.c: Portrait of Safavid Shah Sulaymān (d. 1694), by Shaykh `Abbāsī. Immaculately dressed in stripes, the king sits upright, one hand resting on his jewelled dagger and the other holding up a pink rose. On this right, a small note reads “Shah Sulayman”. The first two years of his reign did not go well. The shah was crowned in late 1666, as Safi II. There then followed so many unlucky events (drought, illness, border raids and a major earthquake) that his officials decided to start again. The palace organised a second coronation, on the more auspicious date of 20 March (Persian New Year, or Norouz) in 1668. The shah’s name also changed, to Sulayman. Per_312.t: Merits of Isfahan (Maḥāsin-e Iṣfahān), by Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Āvīl
Per_312.c: Fine aspects of Isfahan (Mahāsin-e Iṣfahān), Persian translation of al-Māfarrukhī's Arabic original. An important centre of culture, learning and political history, the city of Isfahan held a proud literary tradition of works listing Isfahan’s urban legends, beautiful monuments, famous visitors and local inhabitants. This book also includes descriptions of the city’s parks, and of the pleasures of spring in Isfahan. The author lived in Isfahan in the late eleventh century, and the translator lived there in the fourteenth century. Codex, ink on paper, 155 folios, Persian text in ta`liq script, Fine aspects of Isfahan (Mahāsin-e Iṣfahān), Persian translation by Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad ibn Abi'l-Reẓā al-Ḥusaynī al-Āvī, of Kitāb mahāsin Iṣfahān, a history of Isfahan's sights, marvels, poetry, and famous inhabitants, composed in Arabic c. 1072-1092 by Mufaḍḍal ibn Sa`d ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Māfarrukhī al-Iṣfahānī, incomplete text, unsigned, Iran, undated, c. 1350.

Per_344.t: Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), by Ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371)
Per_344.c: Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), by Ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371). The Safavid shahs were direct descendants of the saintly Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn (died 1334), whose holy tomb at Ardabil for centuries attracted pilgrims, Sufi followers, and shrine patronage. This manuscript is Shaykh Ṣafī's biography, and describes his pious life, sayings and miracles, as well as his family history. Under Shah Ṭahmāsp (r. 1524-1576), a re-worked official version underlined the Ardabil saint’s ancestry, linking his family tree directly back to the Seventh Imam, Mūsā al-Kāẓim (died 799). By extension, this information also transformed the sacred identity of the Safavid shahs themselves, confirming their holy status as sayyids, descended from the Prophet Muḥammad. Codex, ink on paper, 380 folios, Persian text in black nasta`liq script, with red rubrics, Quintessence of Purity (Ṣafvat al-ṣafā’), composed c. 1358 by Tavakkulī ibn Ismā`īl ibn Bazzāz Ardabīlī (d. 1371), biography of Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn Is

Per_378.t: Kashkul, by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī (d. 1621)
Per_378.c: Kashkul, by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī (d. 1621). One of the great intellectuals of Shah `Abbās’s court in Isfahan, Shaykh Bahā’ī was the shah’s leading religious authority. He was a scientist and a poet, and a well-travelled scholar of Islamic law. Entitled Kashkul (the beggar’s bowl), Bahā’ī’s famous anthology gathers entertaining works of poetry, stories, quotations and mathematical proofs. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 144 folios, Persian text in nasta`liq script, with illuminated heading (sarlawh, fols. 1v, 53v, 90v) and leafy gold-painted margins (fols. 1v-2r), Kashkul, literary anthology by Shaykh Bahā’ al-Dīn Muḥammad `Āmilī, known as Shaykh Bahā’ī (Baalbek 1547-1621 or 22 Isfahan), copied by Muḥammad Masīḥ, probably Isfahan, Iran, dated Dhu’l-Hijjah 1076H, June 1666.

Per_395_1.t: Iskandar (Alexander) builds a wall against Gog and Magog, from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma) for Shah Ṭahmāsp, (d. 1576)
Per_395_1.c: Iskandar (Alexander) builds a wall against Gog and Magog, folio from the Book of Divination (Fālnāma). Iskandar sits in conversation with the prophets Khidr and Ilyas (Elijah), while a team of demons (divs) and men toil together to build Iskandar's bronze wall against the monstrous inhabitants of Gog and Magog. This single folio is from a large-scale manuscript of the Book of Divination (Fālnāma), produced for the Safavid Shah Ṭahmāsp, and now dispersed in international collections. There are two folios in the Chester Beatty (CBL Per 395.1 and 395.2). The Fālnāma is not intended to be read from cover to cover, but consulted for divination (as bibliomancy): the seeker opens a page at random, and that chosen page-opening provides the intended augury, in answer to the seeker's question. The text (beginning: "O augury user...") is on the left and a large painting (often depicting sacred figures and prophets) is on the right. For this page-opening, with a scene depicting Alexander the Great

Syc_703.c: Harklean Gospels written in Syriac on parchment in Estrangela script by the scribe Isho’bar Romanos, completed in 1177 at the Church of the Holy Mother (Deipara Maria) situated near Tella d’Arsinos (modern Turkey). It was commissioned by the scribe’s uncle, Rabban Ahron, a priest and monk in Tella. The leather cover is ornamented with interlace borders, interlace cross on the front and an interlaced box on the back, possibly intended to represent the empty tomb. The Gospel book includes the Eusebian letter, canon tables, liturgical lessons, kephalaia (chapters), titles, colophons, and notes from the scribe. The canon tables, which occupy the first ten folios, are contained within architectural frames and decorated with a variety of birds, trees and flowers. This is followed by a stepped cross with interlace ornament and border, echoing the front cover. Square and circular interlaced medallions are found in the lower margin throughout. Syc_705.c: Parchment codex containing an evangeliary or the Nestorian lectionary written in the 12th or 13th century in Syria. It is written in the Estrangela script of Syriac with the title in Arabic on the back. It is bound with blind-tooled and stamped leather covers. Nearly every chapter is decorated with a coloured 'ribbon-over-a-rod' decoration in red, green and yellow.

Syc_709.t: Ephrem's Commentary on the Diatessaron / Letters: Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus (folios 1-10)
Syc_709.c: Parchment manuscript containing two distinct texts written in Syriac. The first ten folios reproduce an exchange of letters between Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus relating to the corruptibility or incorruptibility of the body of Christ. It was written in a mixture of estrangela, nestorian and serta scripts in the 8th or 9th century in Egypt. The remaining sixty-five folios, also produced in Egypt, contain a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in estangela script and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. The two texts were acquired in 1957 and bound together in 1960. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists. Chapters 2.4-9.10 (with some lacunae) are preserved as CBL Syc 709.1. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Syc_709_1.c: Parchment manuscript containing a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in Syriac in estangela script in Egypt and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. It was acquired in two parts, five folios in 1984 and a further 36 in 1986. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 2.4-9.10 (with lacunae at 2.15-20, 3.6-15, 4.2-6 and 7.25-27), the end of Matthew's infancy narrative to Jesus's meeting with Martha and Mary. Chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists are preserved as CBL Syc 709. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Taken together, approximately 80% of the original codex survives (107 of the estimated 134 original folios). The Diatessaron was a gospel harmony written by Tatian (120–173 AD), a second-century Christian theologian. T_406.c: Book of Solomon (Suleymannama) by Sharaf al-Din Musa, Firdausi of Bursa. T_408.t: Forty Sayings of the Prophet (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) by Mir `Ali Shir Nava'i
T_408.c: Forty Sayings of the Prophet (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) by Mir `Ali Shir Nava'i. This beautiful book was copied out in Samarqand by the celebrated calligrapher, Mir `Ali Haravi (meaning from Herat). As well as the exquisite small format calligraphy employed here, Mir `Ali also produced larger scale single-folio "display pieces" (collected in Mughal albums, such as the "Minto Album" folios, CB In 07A), and designs for monumental inscriptions in architectural tilework (for example, at the shrine of Imam Reza in Mashhad). When the political landscape changed with the fall of the Timurid dynasty, Mir `Ali was reportedly conscripted to the court of `Abd al-`Aziz Khan in Bukhara, where he eventually ended his days. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 10 folios, Arabic text, Chaghatay Turkish translation and verse commentary in nasta`liq script, illuminated sarlawh (fol. 1v), gold-flecked borders throughout, Forty Sayings of the Prophet Muhammad (Chehel Hadith-i Rasul) composed after the poet

T_410.c: Evidences of Prophecy (Shavahid al-Nubuvva) by Thana'i An account of the miraculous signs reported for the Prophet, the Caliphs, the Twelve Imams and the Prophet's Companions, gathered together by the author in honour of the Ottoman Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566). T_413.t: History of Sultan Süleyman, by Sayyid Luqman
T_413.c: Concluding History of the Ottoman Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqmān. The Ottoman court historian (şahnameci) Sayyid Luqmān (or Seyyid Lokman) composed this versified account of Süleyman the Magnificent's last seven years of life, describing events in the capital Istanbul, the sultan's military campaigns in the Balkans, Austria, Hungary, on Malta, and on Chios, and concluding with the sultan's death and funeral in 1566. Luqmān was continuing the Ottoman dynastic chronicles established by his two immediate predecessors: Eflatun and before him the renowned court historian `Ārif. `Ārif composed the multi-volume Book of kings of the House of Osman (Shāhnāma-yi Āl-i Osmān): Luqmān’s work (CB T 413) carefully follows this work’s form in language and general layout. `Ārif also worked on two other important accounts of the Ottoman sultan: Mujmal al-Tumar (imperial scroll, 1584) and Hünername (begun 1577), which were completed by his two court successors. T_413_14.c: Iranian envoy bringing diplomatic gifts, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. Here an envoy wearing the Safavid taj turban bows to Sultan Süleyman, flanked very closely by two Ottoman officials. T_413_33.t: Giacomo Cristo, last podesta of Chios, arrested in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman
T_413_33.c: Giacomo Cristo, last podesta of Chios, arrested in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. The podesta was the hereditary governor of the island of Chios, appointed by the Doge of Genoa on behalf of the Genoan republic. Under Ottoman control, the island was ceded and gradually integrated into the imperial administration. At first the podesta continued to rule Chios by paying an annual tribute to Istanbul. In 1566, this tribute was doubled, and the podesta refused to pay. Chios thereafter became an Ottoman sancak territory. The Ottoman court historian (sahnameci) Sayyid Luqman composed this versified account of Süleyman the Magnificent's last seven years of life, describing events in the capital Istanbul, the sultan's military campaigns in the Balkans, Austria, Hungary, on Malta, and on Chios, and concluding with the sultan's death and funeral in 1566. T_413_101.c: Capture of the fortress of Bobofça (Babócsa, Hungary) in 1566, from the History of Sultan Süleyman by Sayyid Luqman. Following the victory over Szigetvar in 1566, the Ottoman army captured the fortress of Bobofça before returning to the capital Istanbul. The sultan had died of natural causes just before the fall of Szigetvar, and his body was now escorted back to Istanbul. W_022.c: Parchment codex containing the Old Testament books Genesis to Ruth written in Latin in black ink around 1153 for Walsingham Priory, Norfolk (England), around the time the monastery was founded. It is the first (and only extant) volume of a complete Bible. Initial letters are written in red, green or blue ink, some with additional pen flourishes. Important texts, rubrics and introductory words are written in alternating green and red. Marginal notes and corrections were added by a contemporary hand in brown ink. Some rubricator notes are still visible in the margins. Each book (or prefatory text) is illustrated with an historiated or decorated initial (10 in total). The manuscript was purchased by Edith Beatty in 1921 from Fitzroy Fenwick (Phillipps Collection 4769) as a gift for Chester Beatty. W_061.c: Bound parchment codex with leather cover preserving a Latin Psalter written in the 13th century in Flanders. The book includes a calendar, psalter, canticles, and litany. There are 12 calendar illustrations depicting abbreviated versions of the labours of the months, 14 full-page miniatures featuring scenes from the Life of the Virgin and the Passion of Jesus Christ, a full-page historiated Beatus initial with 9 additional historiated initials featuring saints, as well as various decorated initials. Each page has bar borders ending in human and animal heads, with other animals and figures in the margins.

W_080.t: Garden of knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia
W_080.c: Parchment codex containing Garden of Knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia, primarily an edited version of Thomas de Cantimpré's On the nature of things (Liber de naturis rerum) with variations and interpolations (including quotations from Gervase of Tilbury), written, edited and illuminated by jurist Jean Reynaud between 1386-1425 probably in Avignon (France). Thomas de Cantimpré (1201-c. 1272) is best known for his encyclopaedia, compiled between 1230-1245, which purported to contain all the natural history knowledge of his time. It included information on anthropology, zoology, botany, mineralogy, astronomy, astrology and meteorology. Jean Reynaud's version took as his model a rare twenty-two book version of Cantimpré's encyclopaedia. The manuscript was purchased in 1924 from the Phillipps Collection.

W_082.c: Illuminated book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. All but four were removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). Removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. On the verso, beneath rubrics in blue, Vespers of the Holy Cross opens with the illuminated initial 'D' (Deus in adiutorium meum intende) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Deposition of Jesus from the cross. W_082_f_133.t: The Trinity from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_133.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). Removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The Psalter of St Jerome is followed by the Athanasian Creed, or Quicunque Vult, which iterates the equality of the three persons of the Trinity. Beneath rubrics in blue, the text opens with the illuminated initial 'Q' (Quicunque vult esse) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Trinity as three bearded men seated upon a throne supported by red seraphim and blue cherubim and/or thrones (both are among the highest order of angels). Each person of the Trinity touches the book with their left hand and gives a gesture of blessing with their right.

It is one of a series of twenty-six prayers to the Virgin Mary in this section of the manuscript.

It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The Star of the Sea prayer concludes on the recto, illuminated in the margin by two angelic musicians. On the verso, beneath rubrics in red, a prayer to the Virgin opens with the illuminated initial ‘G’ (Gaude flore virginalo honoreque) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. It is one of an unusually large series of prayers and paintings dedicated to the Virgin Mary in this manuscript. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Virgin and Child seated on a crescent moon, surrounded by a mandorla and a choir of red seraphim. W_082_f_307.t: Birth of St John the Baptist from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_307.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, a prayer to John the Baptist opens with the illuminated initial ‘O’ (O Johannes gloriose) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Birth of John the Baptist. The main figures are identified in scrolls, perhaps a nod to the fact that Zacharias was deaf. The swaddled infant is held by a midwife or servant, while his mother, Elizabeth, rests in bed after her labour. She is attended by her cousin, the Virgin Mary, along with several unnamed neighbours or relatives. Zacharias writes his son’s name in a book, and t

W_082_f_313.t: Death kneeling before Life from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_313.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, a debate between Life and Death in French opens with the illuminated initial ‘I’ (Je vie royne couronnee) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The debates between Life and Death are some of the numerous additional texts included in this manuscript. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Death kneeling before Life. Death appears as a somewhat fleshy skeleton with two arrows. Life is personified as a Queen, complete with ermine-lined robe, sceptre and crown atop a double-horned headdress (escoffion). The room seems to float in a sea of blue, sep

W_082_f_317.t: Life and Death from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_317.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, Death’s response to Life in French opens with the illuminated initial ‘A’ (A ma tres doulce dame) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The debates between Life and Death are some of the numerous additional texts included in this manuscript. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts Life and Death. Death appears as a somewhat fleshy skeleton with an arrow, and is positioned as if dancing. Life is personified as a Queen with a crown atop a double-horned headdress (escoffion). W_082_f_321.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, the Seven Articles of Faith in French opens with an initial ‘O’ (O glorieuse trinity une essence) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Trinity. The three persons of the Trinity are represented by got with a long white beard, Jesus with a short brunette beard, and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. They are seated in a golden mandorla surrounded by red seraphim, with angels holding a scroll (Sanctus) below. W_082_f_326.t: The Nativity from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_326.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, the first article of faith in French opens with an initial ‘L’ (O tres glorieuse) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Nativity. The Christ Child lays in the centre, illuminated by light from the star. He is surrounded on the left by his kneeling mother Mary, and on the right by Joseph, two shepherds and a donkey and oxen. The Annunciation to the Shepherds is found in the margins. W_082_f_327.t: Baptism of Christ from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_327.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, the second article of faith in French opens with an initial ‘O’ (O vertueux) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Baptism of Christ. Jesus stands in the River Jordan covering his nakedness, his cloak in the hands of an angel, while John the Baptist in his distinctive camel-hair tunic reads from a book and pours water on Christ’s head. The other two parts of the Trinity appear above Christ’s head with the words from God coming from heaven proclaiming his son: hic est filius meus dilectis. In the lower marg

W_082_f_329.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, the third article of faith in French opens with an initial ‘O’ (O vet plons du) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Crucifixion. It is the moment when the lance-bearer, Longinus, pierces Christ’s side. The crowded scene also includes the sponge-bearer, the two thieves, a group of Roman soldiers and the man who recognises Christ, and a group of Jesus’ friends and family identified by their halos. W_082_f_340.t: Harrowing of Hell from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_340.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. Beneath rubrics in red, the fourth article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘O’ (O com joyeuse) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Harrowing of Hell or Decent into Limbo. Christ, attended by angels and holding the resurrection banner, welcomes the souls of the deceased out of the fires of hell, the two figures at the front probably intended to represent Adam and Eve. A demon appears at the back of the group. It is illuminated in the margins by a lion holding the strap of a mirror in its maw, around the mir

W_082_f_342.t: The Resurrection from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_342.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The fourth article of faith in French concludes on the recto, illuminated in the lower margin by the overpainted single charge of the Coëtivy family, one of Prigent’s mottos written around in red, dame sans per (lady without equal) and the Noli me tangere (touch me not). The fifth article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘L’ (Lequint est quil) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Resurrection. Christ steps out of the open tomb with the resurrection banner. W_082_f_349.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The fifth article of faith in French concludes on the recto, illuminated in the margins three figures emerging from flowers in prayer and a choir of angels playing viol, harp and psaltery. The sixth article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘A’ (A douques) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Ascension of Christ. Jesus’ ascension into heaven, his feet just visible, is witnessed by his mother Mary and the twelve apostles, probably John opposite Mary and possibly Peter behind her. W_082_f_356.t: Last Judgement from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_356.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The sixth article of faith in French concludes on the recto, illuminated in the margins by the rescuing of souls from hell. The seventh article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘C’ (Cest article) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Last Judgment. Christ in a mandorla, displaying his wounds and flanked by trumpeting angels, sits on a rainbow as he watches over the rising of souls from their graves below. a: Bourdichon, Jean, attributed to; Fouquet, Jean, follower of; Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to; Master of Jean Charpentier, attributed to; Unknown
W_089.c: A Book of Hours written on parchment and illuminated between 1485-1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. The illuminations are attributed to at least five different hands: the Master of the Echevinage de Rouen (8), Jean Bourdichon (2), a follower of Jean Fouquet (6), the Master of Jean Charpentier (9), and the workshop of the Master of the Echevinage (calendar miniatures and secondary illumination). The pink velvet cover dates to a rebinding, probably in the 17th century. The link with Rouen is confirmed in the suffrages and litany, but not the calendar of feasts. Almost all folios with full-page miniatures were removed from the bound volume in the 20th century. The three miniatures that remain in the book are the Annuncation (f.35r), Harrowing of Hell (f.74r) and Ego sum (f.116v).

W_089_f_13.t: Four Symbols of the Evangelists from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_13.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The four symbols of the evangelists are depicted on a blue ground, each holding a scroll identifying their associated saint: the winged man (S. Matheus), the lion (S. Marcus), the ox (Sanctus Lucas), and the eagle (S. Iohannus). INICIUM SANCTI EVANGELII is written on the golden frame, decorated with acanthus scrolls. The text for the Gospel Lessons, beginning with John, continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains blue flowers.

W_089_f_16.t: Pietà from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_16.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. At the base of a T-shaped cross, a group of women and St John kneel, pray and grief around the body of Jesus which rests on the mantle of his mother Mary. John holds his head. A jar of anointing oils in the lower right is presumably included to identify one of the women as Mary Magdalene. A castle is depicted in the background. OBSECRO TE DOMINA is written on the golden frame, introducing a section of prayers to the Virgin. The rubic, 'cy ensuivent plusieurs honnes et devotes oroisons a nostre dame' is written on the recto below the concluding text to the Gospel Lessons (Mark) which finishes with a decorative line filler.

W_089_f_24.t: Tree of Jesse from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_24.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Jesse sits on a throne with a branching tree rising from behind him. This is a visual representation of the genealogy of Jesus, who depicted as an infant with his mother Mary above. The other ancestors are not identified but generally include Solomon and King David. LIBER GENERACIONIS IHESUS CHIRISTI is written on the gold frame. Lined only on the recto.

W_089_f_30.t: Christ taking leave of his mother from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_30.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The painting depicts Mary kneeling in prayer before a seated Jesus who holds an open book. A group of men are depicted in conversation in the background. The painting introduces the five prayers of St John the Evangelist to the Virgin, announced as Five Sorrows of the Virgin. The rubric on the recto reads, 'Cy ensuivent les cinq douleurs nostre dame contenants cinq resquestes'.

W_089_f_40.t: Visitation from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_40.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Mary stands in a landscape with her cousin Elizabeth who is pregnant with John the Baptist. She kneels as she recognises the significance of Mary's own pregnancy. A city with castle on a hill is depicted across a waterway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] MEU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Lauds of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorated initials introduce different sections of the text, one is decorated with a bird, the other with strawberries.

W_089_f_45.t: Nativity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_45.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. In a stable-like interior with stone walls and wooden roof, a haloed Mary knees before the infant Jesus, Joseph knees behind her. An ox and ass sit behind the infant. Several shepherds, including one playing the bagpipes, watch through windows and the doorway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Prime of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one illustrated with a butterfly, the other with a bird.

W_089_f_47.t: Annunciation to the Shepherds from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_47.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. A night scene, illuminated by heavenly light from above and a camp figure below. A group of shepherds and shepherdesses in a landscape, some holding staffs and one playing the bagpipes, are visited by an angel announcing the birth of Jesus. A city is depicted across a waterway in the background. DUES IN ADIUTORIUM ME[EM] is written on the golden architectural frame, introducing Terce of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Prime of the Virgin. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one depicts a bird, the other a snail.

W_089_f_49.t: Adoration of the Magi from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_49.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Beneath a wooden-framed space, Mary sits with the infant in her lap, Joseph stands behind them. On the left side of the composition, three kings (one who has removed his crown) present gifts to the baby. A star is depicted in the upper left corner, with a riverscape in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words to Sext of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Terce of the Virgin and includes the rubric 'Ad Sextam.'

W_089_f_51.t: The Circumcision from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_51.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Within an interior setting, a group of people crowd around a decorative table (altar). Mary and Joseph stand on the left while a male and female figure hold the infant Jesus as he is circumcised. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM is written on the elaborate golden architectural frame. The text of None of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one with flowers the other with a bird.

W_089_f_53.t: Dormition of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_53.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The apostles stand and kneel around the deathbed of the Virgin Mary. Some hold their hands in prayer while others read from open books, including presumably Peter who also appears to be holding an aspergillum (instrument for sprinkling holy water). Another apostle holds a palm leaf, possibly John. The Resurrected Jesus stands with a staff, both his side and hand wounds visible, and offers a sign of blessing with his left hand. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Vespers of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one encloses a small bird.

W_089_f_54.t: Coronation of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_54.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The Virgin Mary kneels as the Resurrected Jesus, wearing a purple cloak, places a crown on her head, signifying her role as Queen of Heaven. She kneels before God who is depicted as an old man wearing the papal tiara and seated in a covered throne. He holds the orb and cross (globus cruciger). The Holy Spirit in the form of a dove is depicted between God and Jesus. A choir of angels fill the background. CONVERTE NOS DEUS is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words of Compline of the Virgin. The text on the recto includes the concluding prayers for Vespers of the Virgin and the rubric 'Ad completorium'. One two-line decorative initial contains flowers.

W_089_f_57.t: Man of Sorrow from a book of hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_57.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The resurrected Christ stands in his open tomb flanked by the Virgin Mary and St John. The composition may have been inspired by a print of the same subject by Martin Schongauer (1435/50–1491). Written on the bejewelled and gilded trompe-l'oeil frame, D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES, the opening words of Matins of the Holy Cross. The text continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials introduce new sections of text, one enclosing a small bird, the other two contain flowers.

W_089_f_59.t: Pentecost from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_59.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The Virgin Mary with a group of apostles and other women stand in a church-like setting as flaming tongues descend from the upper left. St James the Greater is identified by his pilgrim staff and scallop-emblazoned hat. D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES is written on the frame, which is decorated with a marble effect. The text for Matins of the Holy Spirit continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials open different sections of the text, each contain a small bird.

W_089_f_61.t: Deposition from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_61.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. STABAT MATER DOLOROSA is written on the golden architectural frame. Two men stand on ladders lowering the body of Jesus from the T-shaped cross, aided by a third man (perhaps Joseph of Arimathea) standing in front of the cross. Mary kneels in prayer, John holds the feet of Jesus and a woman (possibly Mary Magdalene) holds his hand. Three other figures are depicted in the background. The text, a hymn to Our Lady of sorrows, continues on the verso, each verse opens with a small decorative initial and each line is finished with decorative line-fillers.

W_089_f_65.t: Bathsheba bathing from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_65.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Bathsheba is seen bathing in a fountain, with King David watching from the window of his castle in the background. DOMINE IN FURORE is written on the gold frame. The text on the verso is from the Penitential Psalms.

W_089_f_89.t: Three persons of the Trinity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_89.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The three figures of God the Father, Jesus and the Holy Spirit are seated in a triple niche with scalloped domes. The each hold an orb and cross (globus cruciger) in one hand and offers a blessing with the other. The central figure is winged. The whole setting appears to be floating. The golden frame is given a marble finish. The text on the verso begins 'Memoire de la benoiste trinite'. A second prayer 'Omnipotens sempiterne deus qui dedisti', opens with the Trinity within the historiated initial O. The text for 'De saint michiel archange' includes St Michael within an historiated initial D.

W_089_f_90.t: St Michael and the Devil from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_90.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. In a landscape, the armoured Archangel Michael fights two demons. One, trapped beneath his feet, attempts to bite the archangel's leg through his armour, the other clings to Michael's shield. No text is written on the golden framed, which is decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves, and therefore the opening words 'MICHAEL ARCHANGELE VENI' are missing from the following prayer. The text on the verso includes prayers to the Archangel Michael and the rubric, 'De monseigneur st michiel larchangel.'

W_089_f_91.t: Archangel Gabriel from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_91.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The Archangel Gabriel, with bejewelled and billowing mantle, holds a cross and scroll which reads, 'Ave gratia plena.' He stands in a large gothic stone cathedral with groin vault. The golden tiles are decorated with blue letters. No text is written on the golden frame, and therefore the first words for the suffrage to the Archangel Gabriel are missing. The text on the recto includes the conclusion of prayers to St Michael and the rubric 'De saint gabriel larchange'. A two-line decorated initial depicts St Micheal.

W_089_f_93.t: St John the Baptist in the wilderness from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_93.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. John the Baptist wearing his camel-hair tunic sits on a rock in a landscape with a sheep. He has a golden halo and holds a cross. PUER QUI NATUS E(ST) NOBIS is written on the bejewelled and gilded frame. The prayer on the verso opens 'Deus qui presentem diem hoborabilem.' St John the Baptist is depicted within the historiated initial D and St Peter is depicted in the historiated initial D, opening a prayer to 'De saint pierre'.

W_089_f_96.t: St George and the Dragon from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen
W_089_f_96.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St George, clothed in golden armour, sits on a white horse from which he slays the dragon. The bones of children the dragon has already eaten in the lower right corner. The princess, whose life is thus saved, stands on the left behind George, while the king and queen (her parents) watch from the top of their castle in the background. SALVE MARTIR GLORIOSE is written in the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Laurence and St Denis and the rubric, 'Memoire de saint george'. Two two-line decorative initials contain the gridiron of St Laurence and the beheaded head of St Denis.

W_089_f_100.t: Martyrdom of St Sebastian from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_100.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Sebastian, tied against a tree, is shot by two archers, multiple arrows already protrude from his body. A figure ties ropes around his feet. Three figures on the left direct the action against Sebastian. A stone, walled city is depicted in the background. O QUAM MIRA REFULSIT GRACIA is written on the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The suffrage to St Sebastian continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains an arrow, the saint's attribute.

W_089_f_101.t: St Martin and the Beggar from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_101.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Martin, sitting on a white horse before the gates to a city, uses his sword to cut his cloak. This is presents to 'the beggar', a man with crutch and wooden leg. Three angels and God hold scrolls written with prayers to the saint. O MARTINE O PIE QUAM PIUM is written on the golden frame. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Nicolas and St Germain and the rubric, 'Memoire de monseigneur saint martin'. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one contains St Nicholas.

W_094.c: A book of hours for the use of Paris in Latin and French, produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. It is written in a gothic script called ‘textualis quadrata’ using dark brown and red ink on parchment and bound in an 18th-century brown leather cover. There are 19 miniatures with realistically-rendered floral borders; 6 remain in the bound volume (ff. 1r, 3r, 11r, 12v, 17r, 23r). Eighteen folios, 14 miniatures (ff.4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 15, 19, 21, 25, 50, 69,126, 211, 242) and 4 text folios (ff.63, 68, 91, 98), were removed from the manuscript around 1954. The book was rebound in the eighteenth century, and pages were repaired and almost certainly removed at that time, likely in response to historic water damage (which is evident throughout the manuscript). A note in French on the fly leaf (f. iiiv), probably written around the time of the rebinding, records the prior removal of several folios with miniatures. W_094_f_04.t: March (recto), Hunting in April (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_04.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for March 15-31, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a particular saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St Benedict of Nursia (21 March) and the Feast of the Annunciation (25 March). On the verso is a hunting scene, introducing the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month,' here associated with April. The ivy-leaf borders are inhabited (in the upper margin) by two putti (wingless cherubs) fighting with shields. In the lower margin, a coat of arms is held between two eagles.

W_094_f_06.t: Enjoying in the Countryside (recto), May (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_06.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of a picnic, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', here associated with May. The borders are filled with realistically-rendered blue violets inhabited (in the upper margin) by a bird. In the lower margin, a coat of arms supported from a pole which rests on the shoulders of two putti (wingless cherubs), each standing on a short, four-legged stool. On the verso is the calendar for May 1-15, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. W_094_f_07.t: May (recto), Hay Harvest in June (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_07.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for May 16-31, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St. Germain of Paris (28 May). On the verso is the hay harvest, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated with June. The border is filled with realistically-rendered holly, inhabited (in the upper margin) by an owl and a pair of water deities. In the lower margin, a coat of arms held by an angel.

W_094_f_09.t: Wheat Harvest (recto), July (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_09.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the wheat harvest, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', here associated with July. The border is filled with realistically-rendered strawberry plants, inhabited by birds, butterflies and putti (wingless cherubs). In the lower margin, a coat of arms held by an angel. On the verso is the calendar for July 1-15, divided into four columns. The most important feasts are written in red, here St. Martin of Tours (4).

On the recto is a scene of threshing and sowing seeds, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated here with November. The border is filled with realistically-rendered blue cornflowers, inhabited by butterflies and, in the upper margin, by a putto (wingless cherubs) with a spear facing a boar. In the lower margin, a coat of arms held between two squirrels. On the verso is the calendar for November 1-15, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. W_094_f_15.t: November (recto), Fattening Pigs and a Banquet in December (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_15.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for November 16-30, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St Clement of Rome (23), St Catherine of Alexandria (25) and St Andrew the Apostle (30). On the verso is a scene of fattening pigs and feasting, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated here with December. The border is filled with realistically-rendered oak leaves and acorns, inhabited, in the upper margin, by a putto (wingless cherubs) holding a shield against a green lizard. In the l

W_094_f_19.t: St Matthew introducing the Gospel lesson of Luke, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_19.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Matthew seated on a canopied throne writing his gospel. His symbol, a winged man, holds the book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue and white columbines (Aquilegia) inhabited by butterflies. A putto with a spear and heron are in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held by two putti below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Luke and his name (lucam) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'In illo tempore, missus est angelus Gabriel a Deo in...' (At that time, the Angel Gabriel was sent of God into...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_21.t: St Luke introducing the Gospel Lesson of Matthew, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_21.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Luke seated before a desk sharpening his pen, a scroll falls over the desk before him. His symbol, a winged ox, rests its hoof on a book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue periwinkles (Vinca) inhabited by birds and butterflies. A putto and bear wrestle in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between two snails below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Matthew and his name (matheum) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'Cum natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem Iuda...' (When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_25.t: The Annunciation introducing Matins of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_25.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Annunciation. While Mary reads, the archangel Gabriel appears and announces her pregnancy. A vase of lilies rest on the floor between then. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted white lilies (Lilium), also known as the Madonna Lily. The tall stems of the flowers twist to create eight roundels in which prophets and ancestors of Mary are painted. The painting introduces Matins of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Domine labia mea aperies' (Lord, you will open my lips). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_50.t: The Visitation introducing Lauds of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_50.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Visitation. Elizabeth, pregnant with John the Baptist, embraces her also pregnant cousin Mary. They stand in a landscape, while Joseph walks out of the frame to the left. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted strawberries (Fragaria) inhabited by butterflies. A putto plays with a dog, while a cat hisses in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between a dog and cat below. The painting introduces Lauds of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries.

W_094_f_63.t: Prime of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_63.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the verso is an historiated initial V with a half-length portrait of a man wearing an ermine-trimmed cloak. This is probably meant to represent King David, to whom the psalms are traditionally ascribed. The text which follows is from psalm 5, and begins Verba mea auribus percipe (Hear my words). The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains. The mound on the verso is home to a life-like rat.

W_094_f_68.t: Terce of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_68.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the recto is an historiated initial P with a half-length portrait of a nude woman. She is probably meant to represent Eve. The text which follows reads Paradisi porta per evam, and continues on the verso, cunctis clausa est. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders created with chains.

W_094_f_69.t: The Adoration of the Magi introducing Sext of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_69.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the concluding text for the hour of Terce of the Virgin. The rubic for Sext of the Virgin (Ad vi) is written in red at the bottom. The text is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries. On the verso is a scene of the Adoration of the Magi. May holds the baby Jesus while a procession of figures on horses come to great them with gifts. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted boxwood leaves (Boxus) inhabited by butterflies. A dog faces a porcupine in the upper margin while two bears hold the coat of arms in the lower margin. The painting introduces Sext of the Virgin, usually read around noon. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me).

W_094_f_91.t: The Penitential Psalms, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_91.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Penitential Psalms. The recto includes text from psalm 50 which concludes on the verso. The is followed by the Latin word psalmus is written in red and the beginning of psalm 101; Domine exaudi orationem meum (Lord, hear my prayer). Both sides of the folio are decorated with conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised flowers.

W_094_f_98.t: The Litany, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_98.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Litany, which includes invocations for the intercession of various saints. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains.

W_094_f_126.t: The Office of the Dead, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_126.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Office of the Dead. On the recto an historiated initial A contains a grotesque bird with leaves emanating from its beak. The text is from psalm 119 and begins Ad dominum cum tribularer clamavi (When I was in tribulation I cried to our Lord). The text continues on the verso. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves and suns in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains.

W_094_f_211.t: The Raising of the Cross introducing Sext of the Passion, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_211.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Raising of the Cross or Crucifixion. Jesus is nailed to the cross positioned diagonally across the picture as it is raised upright. The scene is crowded with soldiers and other onlookers. His mother Mary and friends grieve in the lower right. A ship sails on rough waters in the background. The painting is surrounded by blue larkspurs inhabited above by a putto facing a rearing long-horned goat. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two donkeys. The scene introduces Sext of the Passion (to be read at noon), and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers and acanthus leaves.

W_094_f_242.t: The Baptism of Jesus introducing a prayer to John the Baptist, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_242.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Baptism of Jesus by his cousin John the Baptist. Jesus stands in the Jordan River looking over his shoulder toward God who holds open a book. An angel looks down from mountains above. The painting is surrounded by pink roses inhabited by putti. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two wildmen. The scene introduces a prayer to John the Baptist and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers.

W_099.c: A rosarium codex written in Latin on parchment with miniatures painted by Simon Bening (1483-1561) made between 1540-1545 in Bruges. The codex is bound in a sixteenth-century Spanish gold-tooled leather binding with two metal clasps. A number of its miniatures were removed from the binding and are now housed separately. A rosarium is a collection of devotions dedicated to the Virgin Mary. One of the most conspicuous features of this richly illuminated example is its purple margins, a distinctive mark of royal ownership. Indeed, this illuminated rosarium was commissioned by either the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (1500–1558) or his son, Philip II, King of Spain (1527–1598). The paintings are the work of Simon Bening, the last of the great masters of Flemish manuscript painting. Bening drew inspiration from his peers, quoting freely from Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer, and he in turn influenced the next generation of artists.
